text_src:
⸢In the beginning⸣: Using the same phrase as the beginning of the Old Testament (Genesis 1:1), the Gospel of John introduces Jesus Christ as the one through whom God created everything (John 1:3). Through Jesus, God also creates new life in those who believe (1:12–13). 

The Gospel of John begins with its central claim: Jesus Christ, the Word (⸢logos⸣), not only revealed God but was God. The Greek word ⸢logos⸣ means “word” or “message.” The ⸢logos⸣ is the Word of God, through whom God created everything, made himself known, and became human as Jesus Christ. Later Christian teaching describes the Word as the second person of the Trinity (the one who shares fully in God’s nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit).

In Greek thought, the ⸢logos⸣ was the rational principle that ordered the universe and made life understandable. It explained why the world had meaning and structure.

For Jewish people, the ⸢logos⸣ was the word of the Lord. It expressed God’s wisdom and God’s creative power. God spoke, and things came into being.

By the time of Jesus, people understood the ⸢logos⸣ as coming from God and sharing God’s character and authority (see Psalm 33:6, 9; Proverbs 8:22–31). John affirmed this understanding by declaring that "the Word [⸢logos⸣] became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14).
text_es_aquifer: Reflejando Gen 1:1, el Evangelio de Juan presenta a Jesucristo, a través de quien Dios creó todo (Jn 1:3); Jesús también crea nueva vida en aquellos que creen (1:12–13). El Evangelio comienza con su afirmación central, que Jesucristo, la Palabra (⸢logos ⸣en griego), no solo reveló a Dios sino que era Dios en si misma⸢.⸣ En el pensamiento griego, el ⸢logos⸣ era el principio racional que guiaba el universo y daba coherencia a la vida. Para los judíos, el logos era la palabra del Señor, una expresión de la sabiduría y el poder creativo de Dios. Para la época de Jesús, el logos se veía como proveniente de Dios y con su personalidad (ver Sal 33:6, 9, Pr 8:22–31); Juan afirmó este entendimiento (Jn 1:14).El ⸢logos ⸣es la Palabra de Dios, a través de la cual Dios creó todo, se dio a conocer y se hizo humano como Jesucristo. Las enseñanzas cristianas posteriores describen a la Palabra como la segunda persona de la Trinidad (aquella que comparte plenamente la naturaleza de Dios con el Padre y el Espíritu Santo).

text_src:
The start of this introduction might be a poem or hymn sung by early Christians (1:1–5). 

The themes of this introduction of the Gospel of John prepare readers for the story that follows:The arrival of the light in the world.The rejection of the light.The gift of new life given by the light to those who believed in him.
text_es_aquifer: El comienzo de este prólogo (1.1–5) podría ser un poema o un himno cantado por los primeros cristianos. Los temas del prólogo: la llegada de la luz al mundo, el rechazo de la luz y su don de nueva vida a los creyentes, preparan a los lectores para la historia que sigue.

text_src: The Word (⸢logos⸣) is God (1:1–2). Everything God does, the Word also does. Throughout his Gospel, John presents the actions of Jesus as the actions of God himself.
text_es_aquifer: El ⸢logos ⸣es Dios (1.1–2); todo lo que Dios hace, el ⸢logos⸣ también lo hace. A lo largo de su Evangelio, Juan consideró correctamente las acciones de Jesús como actividad divina.

text_src: ⸢In Him was life⸣: Life was God’s original gift to his creatures at creation (Genesis 1:20–28; 2:7). Now the ⸢logos⸣ gives people the possibility of new life, which comes through rebirth from God (John 1:13). This means receiving new life from God, not a second physical birth. It describes a spiritual beginning in which God gives people new life through faith, making them his childrenAs one of his first creative acts, God brought light into the world (Genesis 1:3). In the re-creation of humankind through Jesus Christ, God offered light and life again. Light is a key theme throughout the Gospel of John.
text_es_aquifer: "La Palabra dio vida": La vida fue el regalo original de Dios a sus criaturas (Gn 1.20–28, 2.7). Ahora el ⸢logos ⸣daría a estas criaturas la posibilidad de una nueva vida a través del nuevo nacimiento (Jn 1.13). • Como uno de sus primeros actos de creación, Dios trajo luz (Gn 1.3). Ahora, en la recreación de la humanidad a través de Jesucristo, Dios ofreció luz y vida de nuevo. La luz es un tema clave en el Evangelio de Juan.

text_src: God created ⸢light⸣ and removed the ⸢darkness⸣ (Genesis 1:2–5). The darkness resists God (John 3:19–21; 12:35; Matthew 6:23; Acts 26:17–18; Ephesians 4:17–19; 5:7–14; 2 Peter 1:19; 1 John 1:5–7; 2:9–11).
text_es_aquifer: Dios creó la luz y disipó las tinieblas (Gn 1.2–5). Las tinieblas resisten a Dios (Juan 3.19–21, 12.35, Mat 6.23, Hec 26.17–18, Ef 4.17–19, 5.7–14, 2 Pe 1.19, 1 Jn 1.5–7, 2.9–11).

lemma_src: the darkness has not overcome it
text_src: ⸢the darkness has not overcome it⸣:  Or ⸢the darkness has not understood it; ⸣literally, ⸢the darkness cannot grasp it⸣. The Greek word ⸢katalambanō⸣ (“grasp”) can mean either “understand” or “be hostile.” In John’s Gospel, it means "hostility." The darkness would try to destroy Jesus (the Light), but it would fail. The Light would successfully bring salvation to the world.
text_es_aquifer: "las tinieblas no prevalecieron contra la luz": O "las tinieblas no lo han entendido"⸢;⸣ literalmente "la oscuridad no puede comprenderlo"⸢.⸣ La palabra griega ⸢katalambanō ⸣(“comprender”) puede significar tanto “entender” como “ser hostil”; en el Evangelio de Juan, significa hostilidad. La oscuridad intentaría destruir a Jesús (la luz), pero fracasaría. La luz traería con éxito la salvación al mundo.

text_src: God sent a man named John the Baptist to announce the arrival of Jesus. He prepared people to accept Jesus as God's Son and Messiah (see 1:19–37; Luke 1:5–25, 57–80; 3:1–22). His work fulfilled what God had promised through the prophets (see Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 4:5–6).
text_es_aquifer: Dios envió a un hombre, Juan el Bautista, para anunciar la venida de Jesús y preparar al pueblo de Dios para recibir a Jesús como el Hijo de Dios y el Mesías (ver 1:19–37, Lc 1:5–25, 57–80; 3:1–22, ver también Is 40:3, Ml 4:5–6).

text_src: Some Jews thought John the Baptist might be the Messiah (God's chosen one). Some of his followers hesitated to follow Jesus (3:22–30). However, John the Baptist was not the Light. His role was to announce Jesus (1:19–34).
text_es_aquifer: Algunos judíos especulaban que Juan el Bautista era el Mesías; algunos de sus seguidores incluso eran reacios a seguir a Jesús (3.22–30). Sin embargo, Juan el Bautista no era la luz⸢,⸣ su papel era anunciar a Jesús (1.19–34).

text_src: The world does not recognize the true light, even when meeting its Creator. The world lives in rebellion, loving darkness more than light (3:19).
text_es_aquifer: El mundo no puede reconocer la verdadera luz incluso cuando encuentra a su Creador. El mundo vive en rebelión, amando más la oscuridad que la luz (3.19).

text_src: People can follow the light and join God's family only when God spiritually renews them (3:1–17). People must believe in Christ to become children of God (12:35–36).
text_es_aquifer: Solo a través de la renovación divina las personas pueden seguir la luz y entrar en la familia de Dios (3.1–17). • Los individuos deben creer en Cristo para convertirse en hijos de Dios (12.35–36).

text_src: ⸢born of God⸣: People can escape the darkness only by God’s grace (see 8:12; 12:35–36, 44–46).
text_es_aquifer: "Un nacimiento que viene de Dios": Las personas pueden escapar de la oscuridad sólo por la gracia de Dios (8.12, 12.35–36, 44–46).

text_src:
⸢The Word became flesh⸣: This means the Word became truly human. The idea that the Word became human was shocking to both Greeks and Jews. 

Many Greeks believed that God was completely separate from the ordinary human world. They used the word ⸢sarx⸣ (Greek for “flesh”) to describe human life as weak or earthly. John taught something very different. He said that God himself became human in Jesus Christ (compare 1:1). 

Jesus was fully human and fully divine. He was not partly God and partly human. These two truths together form the foundation of Christian teaching about Christ.⸢the Word … made His dwelling among us⸣ (Greek ⸢skēnoō,⸣ “pitched a tent”): The Greek verb ⸢skēnoō⸣ means “to pitch a tent” or “to live in a tent.” This word is related to ⸢skēnē⸣, the Greek word for the tabernacle. The tabernacle was the tent where the Lord’s glory lived among Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 25:8–9). In Jesus, God’s glory now lived among his people in a new way (Exodus 40:34–38; John 2:11; 12:23–28, 41; 17:1–5). Even though the world was dark and hostile, Jesus came to save it. He offered God’s love and faithfulness to the world (3:15–17).
text_es_aquifer: La idea de que el Verbo se hizo humano (literalmente "se hizo carne") sorprendió tanto a griegos como a judíos. Los griegos separaban la esfera de Dios del mundo mundano de la humanidad, al que llamaban "carne" (del griego ⸢sarx⸣). Juan escribió que Dios mismo se hizo "carne" en Cristo (cp. 1.1). La humanidad y divinidad de Jesús eran completas, no parciales. Las dos ideas, Jesús como 100 por ciento divino y 100 por ciento humano, forman la base de la comprensión cristiana de Cristo. • "la Palabra . . . hizo su hogar (del griego ⸢skēnoō,⸣ “plantó su tienda”) entre nosotros": esta palabra griega está relacionada con la palabra usada para el Tabernáculo del Antiguo Testamento (del griego ⸢skēnē,⸣ “tienda, tabernáculo”), la tienda en el desierto donde residía la gloria del Señor y donde Israel venía a adorar (Ex 25.8–9). La gloria del Padre en el Tabernáculo (Ex 40.34–38) estaba ahora presente en Jesucristo (Juan 2.11, 12.23–28, 41; 17.1–5). • Jesús ofreció el amor y la fidelidad infalibles de Dios. A pesar de la oscuridad hostil del mundo, Jesús entró en el mundo para salvarlo (3.15–17).

text_src:
⸢He was before m⸣e: In John the Baptist’s culture, older age was respected and honored (Leviticus 19:32). Younger people were expected to honor those who were older, not replace them (contrast Isaiah 3:5). 

By saying that Jesus existed before him, John the Baptist pointed to the greater honor of Jesus. He explained that Jesus existed before creation itself, not just before the birth of John (John 1:1–3).
text_es_aquifer: "él existió mucho antes que yo": En una sociedad donde la edad era respetada y honrada (Lv 19.32, contraste Is 3.5), Juan el Bautista enfatizó el honor de Jesús señalando su existencia incluso antes de la creación (Jn 1.1–3).

text_src: ⸢the law⸣: This refers to the ⸢Torah⸣, the body of instruction given to Moses at Mount Sinai. The Torah taught Israel how to live in faithful relationship with God and with one another.God's grace and truth are present in the Torah, but Jesus fully reveals these qualities in his person and power (3:16; 13:1).
text_es_aquifer: "la ley": es decir, la ⸢torah⸣, el conjunto de instrucciones dado a Moisés en el Monte Sinaí. • Aunque el amor inquebrantable y la fidelidad de Dios están en la ⸢torah⸣, estas cualidades se revelan completamente en Cristo (3.16, 13.1).

lemma_src: but the one and only Son
text_src: God would not allow Moses to see him directly (Exodus 33:18–20). Only Jesus has seen the Father, so he alone completely knows him and can tell us about him (John 3:32–35; 14:9–10). ⸢but the one and only Son⸣: The Son, who sees the Father, ⸢is himself God. ⸣The Son is not simply a messenger who knows something about God. John explicitly affirms Christ’s deity. Jesus shares the substance of God’s being.
text_es_aquifer: Moisés tuvo negado su deseo de ver a Dios directamente (Ex 33.18–20). Solo Jesús ha visto al Padre, por lo que solo él lo conoce completamente y puede contarnos sobre él (Juan 3.32–35, 14.9–10). • "Pero el Único, que es él mismo Dios": el Hijo, que ve al Padre, "es él mismo Dios"⸢, ⸣no simplemente un mensajero que sabe algo sobre Dios. Juan afirma explícitamente la deidad de Cristo. Jesús comparte la sustancia del ser de Dios.

text_src:
John’s Gospel focuses less on John the Baptist compared to the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew 3:1–6; Mark 1:2–6; Luke 1:1–24, 57–80; 3:1–13). However, the apostle John wants us to understand that John the Baptist correctly identified and honored Jesus. 

John the Baptist’s disciples leave him to follow Jesus. Jesus continued the work that John had begun. As the ministry of Jesus grew, John’s ministry became smaller, just as John had said (John 3:30).
text_es_aquifer: El Evangelio de Juan presta poca atención a Juan el Bautista en comparación con los evangelios sinópticos (Mateo 3:1–6, Marcos 1:2–6, Lucas 1:1–24, 57–80; 3:1–13). Sin embargo, el apóstol Juan quiere que veamos que Juan el Bautista identificó y exaltó correctamente a Jesús. Los discípulos de Juan el Bautista lo dejan y siguen a Jesús; Jesús asumió el ministerio que Juan comenzó, creciendo mientras Juan disminuía (Juan 3:30).

text_src: Jesus reveals himself to the world through his miracles and teachings. People reacted differently:Some wanted to believe in him.Others opposed him. This division becomes more obvious as the book continues. Jesus ended his public ministry with a final call for people to believe in him (12:44–50).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús se revela al mundo a través de sus señales milagrosas y sermones. El público estaba dividido: algunos querían creer en él; otros se oponían a él. Esta división se intensifica a medida que avanza el libro. Jesús terminó su ministerio público con un último llamado a que la gente creyera en él (12.44–50).

text_src: The Jews expected the Christ (the Greek form of the Hebrew word ⸢Messiah⸣) to bring spiritual leadership and political redemption to Israel. Both words mean “Anointed One” (a king chosen and set apart by God). They believed this promised leader would guide them back to faithful worship and free them from foreign rule (see Deuteronomy 18:15; see also the Jewish book ⸢Psalms of Solomon ⸣from the period between the Old and New Testaments).
text_es_aquifer: Los judíos esperaban que el Mesías (la forma hebrea de la palabra griega "Cristo") trajera liderazgo espiritual y redención política a Israel (ver Deut 18.15, ver también el libro judío intertestamentario ⸢Salmos de Salomón⸣).

text_src: The people expected Elijah to come before the Messiah (Malachi 4:5). John the Baptist fulfilled this role as the forerunner (the one who prepares the way). However, John said that he was not Elijah himself (see Matthew 11:14; Luke 1:17). ⸢Are you the Prophet?⸣: Compare John 6:14; 7:40–41.
text_es_aquifer: Elías iba a ser el precursor del Mesías (Mal 4.5). Juan el Bautista cumplió el papel de precursor, aunque negó ser el profeta Elías (ver Mat 11.14, Lc 1.17). • "¿Eres tú el Profeta que estamos esperando?" Cf. Juan 6.14, 7.40–41.

text_src: ⸢Who are you?⸣: John the Baptist wanted others to know him as ⸢a voice of one calling in the wilderness⸣ (see Isaiah 40:3).
text_es_aquifer: "Entonces, ¿quién eres tú?" Juan el Bautista simplemente quería ser conocido como una voz que clama en el desierto (ver Is 40.3).

text_src:
The Pharisees were deeply devoted to the Scriptures and earnestly desired a righteous life. They also believed in the coming Messiah, which explains their questions here. 

Some Pharisees became followers of Jesus, including the apostle Paul (Acts 15:5; 26:5; Philippians 3:5).
text_es_aquifer: Los fariseos estaban dedicados profundamente a las Escrituras y deseaban sinceramente una vida justa. También creían en la venida del Mesías, lo que explica sus preguntas aquí. Algunos fariseos se convirtieron en creyentes en Jesús (Hec 15.5), incluido el apóstol Pablo (Hec 26.5; Fil 3.5).

text_src: Jewish baptisms were ritual washings for becoming ceremonially pure following contact with impurity (Leviticus 8:6; Numbers 19:7). John announced the Christ's arrival and required participants to confess their sins and be baptized (Matthew 3:6). Baptism later became the symbol of membership in the kingdom of God (Acts 2:38; see also John 4:1–2).
text_es_aquifer: Los bautismos judíos eran lavados rituales para volverse ceremonialmente puros después del contacto con la impureza (Lv 8:6, Nm 19:7). • El anuncio de Juan sobre la llegada del Mesías requería que los participantes confesaran sus pecados y se bautizaran (Mt 3:6). El bautismo más tarde se convirtió en el símbolo de la membresía en el reino de Jesús (Hc 2:38; ver también Jn 4:1–2).

text_src: A slave usually did simple tasks like removing a sandal⸢. ⸣A disciple never did these tasks.
text_es_aquifer: Una tarea servil como quitar una sandalia estaba reservada para un esclavo⸢;⸣ estas tareas nunca eran realizadas por un discípulo.

text_src: The phrase ⸢the Lamb of God⸣ may refer to the Passover sacrifice of a lamb or to the daily sacrifice in the temple (Exodus 29:38–46; Hebrews 10). See also Revelation 5.
text_es_aquifer: La frase "Cordero de Dios" podría referirse al sacrificio de un cordero en la Pascua o al sacrificio diario en el Templo (Éxodo 29:38–46, Hebreos 10). Véase también Apocalipsis 5.

text_src:
John the Baptist's second testimony (see 1:19–23) describes what happened when he baptized Jesus . In the Old Testament, kings and prophets were anointed with the Holy Spirit. These anointings were temporary. They were given for a specific task or time.

By contrast, the Spirit remained on Jesus. His anointing was not temporary. It was permanent (see 3:34).
text_es_aquifer: El segundo testimonio de Juan el Bautista (ver 1.19–23) contó lo que sucedió cuando Jesús fue bautizado. • En el Antiguo Testamento, los reyes y profetas eran ungidos con el Espíritu Santo⸢,⸣ pero estas unciones eran temporales y estaban ligadas a un cargo u ocasión particular. En cambio, con el Espíritu reposando sobre él, la unción de Jesús fue permanente (ver 3.34).

text_src: ⸢the Son of God⸣: Some ancient manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God,” which echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God speaks of his chosen servant.
text_es_aquifer: "el Elegido de Dios": ver Is 42.1.

text_src: This section introduces the model for discipleship in John’s Gospel. Disciples wanted to come and see Jesus, and when they met him, they stayed with him (1:39).
text_es_aquifer: Esta sección introduce el modelo de discipulado en el Evangelio de Juan. Los discípulos deseaban venir y ver a Jesús (1.39), y cuando lo encontraron, permanecieron con él.

text_src: Simon is well known in the Gospels, not for his courage and faith, but for his failings (see 18:15–18, 25–27). Jesus gave him the name ⸢Cephas⸣, an Aramaic word that means “rock.” In Greek, this name is ⸢Petros⸣. In English, we say Peter. This name pointed to the strong church leader Simon would later become (see Acts 1:1–5:42; 8:1–12:25; 15:1–41).
text_es_aquifer: Simón es bien conocido en los Evangelios, no por su valentía y fe, sino por sus fallos (ver 18.15–18, 25–27). Jesús lo nombró Cefas (“la roca”), refiriéndose al gran líder de la iglesia que llegaría a ser más tarde (ver Hechos 1.1–5:42, 8.1–12:25, 15.1–41).

text_src: Galilee was the region of northern Israel around the Sea of Galilee.Bethsaida was a village on Galilee's north shore. The name ⸢Bethsaida⸣ means "house of fishing." It was the home of Peter, Andrew, and Philip. Later, Andrew and Peter moved to Capernaum, a village west of Bethsaida (Mark 1:21, 29).
text_es_aquifer: Galilea era la región del norte de Israel alrededor del mar de Galilea. • Betsaida (“casa de pesca”) era un pueblo en la costa norte de Galilea y el hogar de Pedro, Andrés y Felipe. Más tarde, Pedro y Andrés se mudaron a Capernaum, un pueblo al oeste de Betsaida (Marcos 1.21, 29).

text_src: Philip⸢,⸣ a Greek name, and Nathanael⸢,⸣ a Hebrew name, represent the mix of cultures in Galilee. The message of Jesus reached both groups in Galilee. When Greeks wanted to see Jesus in Jerusalem, they asked Philip (12:20–22). Jesus grew up in Nazareth, a mountain village southwest of the Sea of Galilee.
text_es_aquifer: Felipe⸢,⸣ un nombre griego, y Natanael⸢,⸣ un nombre hebreo, representan la mezcla de culturas en Galilea. El mensaje de Jesús allí se dirigía a ambos públicos. Cuando los griegos querían ver a Jesús en Jerusalén, se acercaron a Felipe (12.20–22). • Jesús creció en Nazaret⸢,⸣ un pueblo montañoso al suroeste del mar de Galilea.

lemma_src: Can anything good come from Nazareth?
text_src: ⸢Can anything good come from Nazareth?⸣: People did not think this village was important enough to be the hometown of a great leader (see Matthew 13:53–58).
text_es_aquifer: "¿Puede salir algo bueno de Nazaret?" Este pueblo no se consideraba lo suficientemente famoso como para ser la ciudad natal de un gran líder (cp. Mateo 13.53–58).

text_src:
Jesus described Nathanael as ⸢a true Israelite⸣. He said there was no deceit (no dishonesty or trickery) in him.

This may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, whose early life was marked by deceit. Jacob later received the name ⸢Israel⸣ (see Genesis 25:27–34; 27:1–36; 32:22–32). In this way, Nathanael shows what God desires Israel to be. God wants his people to be an honest and faithful people.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús se refirió a Natanael como un hombre de total integridad⸢,⸣ contrastándolo con Jacob, el patriarca astuto y engañoso a quien Dios renombró Israel (ver Gn 25.27–34, 27.1–36, 32.22–32). Es como si Natanael encarnara el ideal de Dios para Israel.

text_src:
Jesus gained Nathanael’s attention by showing that he knew his character (1:47). Then Jesus showed that he knew Nathanael’s earlier actions, even though they had not met before.

This supernatural knowledge (knowledge beyond normal human ability) amazed Nathanael. He saw this as a sign from God and responded with faith.

Nathanael had witnessed a miracle. As a result, he made a strong confession about who Jesus is.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús llamo la atención de Natanael porque conocía su carácter (1.47), luego ganó la adoración de Natanael al saber sobrenaturalmente sus acciones anteriores. Natanael presenció un milagro y dio un paso notable de fe.

text_src:
⸢Truly, truly⸣ (Greek ⸢amēn amēn⸣): Jesus often used this phrase to emphasize important points. In John’s Gospel, the Greek word ⸢amēn⸣ is always doubled. ⸢you will all see heaven open⸣: Jesus made the comparison with Jacob clear (see study note on 1:47; see Genesis 28:10–22). Like Jacob, Nathanael would see God at work. Jacob saw a vision at Bethel, where God revealed himself (Genesis 28:19). 

Jesus himself is the new Bethel. The name ⸢Bethel⸣ means “house of God.” In other words, Jesus is the place where God now lives among his people.⸢Son of Man⸣: See study note on John 9:35; see also Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 8:31. John the apostle used several names for Jesus (Son of God, Son of Man, Christ). Knowing the true identity of Jesus is necessary to fully understanding and following him.
text_es_aquifer: Les digo la verdad (del griego ⸢amēn amēn⸣): Jesús a menudo usaba esta expresión para enfatizar lo que estaba a punto de decir. En el Evangelio de Juan, la palabra griega ⸢amēn ⸣siempre está duplicada. • "todos verán el cielo abierto": Jesús hizo explícita la comparación con Jacob (ver nota de estudio en 1.47, ver Gn 28.10–22). Como Jacob, Natanael vería a Dios en acción. Jesús mismo es el nuevo ⸢Betel ⸣(“casa de Dios,” Gn 28.19), el lugar donde Dios vive. • "Hijo del Hombre": ver nota de estudio en Juan 9.35; ver también Dn 7.13–14; Mar 8.31. • El apóstol Juan usó varios nombres para Jesús (Hijo de Dios, Hijo del Hombre, Mesías). Conocer la verdadera identidad de Jesús es necesario para comprenderlo y seguirlo plenamente.

text_src: ⸢Wedding⸣ ceremonies could last up to a week. They often included dramatic parades where the husband brought the bride to his home for the celebrations (Matthew 25:1–13).
text_es_aquifer: Las ceremonias que rodean la celebración de una boda podrían durar hasta una semana; las bodas a menudo incluían procesiones dramáticas en las que el novio llevaba a la novia a su casa para las festividades (Mat 25.1–13).

text_src: In this section, Jesus appeared at two symbolic Jewish ceremonies. At a wedding in Cana (2:1–12), he replaced the ritual cleansing water with his own superior wine. Later, around Passover, he cleansed the temple (2:13–25).
text_es_aquifer: En esta sección, Jesús apareció en dos ceremonias judías  simbólicas. En la boda en Caná (2.1–12), reemplazó el agua de los rituales de purificación con su propio vino superior. Más tarde, alrededor de la Pascua, limpió el Templo (2.13–25).

text_src: Jesus showed who he is and what he came to do through the religious practices and festivals of the Jewish people (see 2:1; 5:1). He used these familiar events to reveal his identity and his mission.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús ilustró su identidad y obra a través de las instituciones y los festivales del judaísmo (ver 2.1, 5.1).

text_src: When the wine supply ran out⸢,⸣ the host’s family would face embarrassment for failure to plan properly. Perhaps Jesus arrived unexpectedly with his disciples (see Matthew 25:1–13). This might explain why his mother told him about the problem. A wedding feast was a major celebration in Jewish village life. This particular event also symbolized the joy of the Messiah's arrival.
text_es_aquifer: Cuando se acabó el suministro de vino⸢,⸣ la familia del anfitrión enfrentaría vergüenza por no planificar adecuadamente. Tal vez Jesús llegó inesperadamente (cp. Mat 25.1–13), trayendo su círculo de discípulos, lo que podría explicar por qué su madre le llevó el problema. • El banquete de bodas era la principal celebración en la vida del pueblo judío, y este episodio simbolizaba también la alegría por la llegada del Mesías.

lemma_src: My hour has not yet come
text_src: At first, Jesus did not step in to solve the problem. His mission and its timing were not controlled by human plans.⸢My hour has not yet come⸣: This refers to the time when Jesus would be glorified. In the Gospel of John, this happened when he was lifted up on the cross (12:23; 17:1).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús inicialmente se distanció del problema. Su misión y su tiempo no podían ser establecidos por una agenda humana. • El tiempo de Jesús (literalmente "hora") llegaría en el futuro cuando sería glorificado al ser levantado en la cruz (12.23, 17.1).

text_src:
The stone water jars were cut from solid rock. They were used for Jewish purification ceremonies (religious washing rituals; see Mark 7:1–4).

Jesus was about to give new meaning to these ceremonies. He would show that something greater than ritual washing was now present.
text_es_aquifer: Talladas en roca maciza, las jarras de agua de piedra se utilizaban para ceremonias religiosas de lavado (ver Marcos 7.1–4). Jesús estaba a punto de llenar la ceremonia judía con un nuevo contenido.

text_src:
The master of the banquet repeated a common saying. Normally, the best wine was served first, when people could taste it most clearly. Later, wine of lower quality was served.

But this time it was different. The wine Jesus made, served last, was the best of all.

In the Old Testament, good wine was a sign of God’s blessing(Amos 9:13–14). This miracle showed that the Messiah, God’s greatest blessing, had now come.
text_es_aquifer: El maestro de ceremonias citó un proverbio. El mejor vino siempre se servía primero cuando los paladares eran más sensibles; sin embargo, este vino milagroso, servido al final, era el mejor. El buen vino simbolizaba la bendición de Dios (Am 9.13–14). El Mesías, la mayor bendición de Dios, al fin había llegado.

text_src: ⸢Jesus performed this, the first of His signs⸣: In it, he revealed the glory of God  (see also 1:14; 11:4, 40).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús había ofrecido su primera señal milagrosa. En ella, reveló la gloria de Dios (véase también 1.14, 11.4, 40).

text_src: The Jewish Passover was an annual spring feast remembering Israel’s rescue from slavery in Egypt (Exodus 12). Jews traveled to Jerusalem to join the feast (Deuteronomy 16:1–16). Because John refers to three Passover feasts (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55), many scholars think Jesus must have had a three-year public ministry.
text_es_aquifer: La Pascua⸢,⸣ un festival anual de primavera, conmemoraba el rescate de Israel de la esclavitud en Egipto (Ex 12). Los judíos viajaban a Jerusalén para participar en el festival (Deut 16.1–16). Por causa de que Juan se refiere a tres festivales de Pascua (Juan 2.13, 6.4; 11.55), muchos concluyen que Jesús tuvo un ministerio público de tres años.

text_src:
Many people came to Jerusalem for the Passover festival. They needed animals that met the requirements for sacrifice. The animals had to be approved for worship.

Because of this need, a large business developed. People sold animals and exchanged money for the right kind of coins. However, this buying and selling was taking place in the temple itself.

Jesus acted like a prophet. He demanded that God’s house return to its true purpose. The temple was meant for worship, prayer, teaching, and sacrifice. It was not meant to be a marketplace. This action brought Jesus into conflict with the temple leaders.The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) place the clearing out of the temple near the end of the ministry of Jesus (Matthew 21:12–13; Mark 11:15–17; Luke 19:45–46). John might have included this event earlier to emphasize its connection to the miracle where Jesus turned water into wine (John 2:1–11). Both the temple and the stone jars of water were instruments for spiritual purity in Judaism. The jars, once filled with water for ceremonial washing, now held the wine Jesus changed by a miracle. 

In a similar way, the stone temple, which was linked to sacrifice and purification, would no longer be central. Jesus himself would take its place (2:19–21). 

Some scholars believe that Jesus cleansed the temple twice. They think he did this once at the beginning of his ministry and again at the end.
text_es_aquifer: Los que venían para la Pascua necesitaban tener sacrificios aprobados para el culto. De esta necesidad surgió una considerable industria de venta de animales e intercambio de dinero; además, este negocio se llevaba a cabo en el Templo. Jesús, como un profeta, exigió que la casa de Dios volviera a sus usos previstos: adoración, oración, instrucción y sacrificio. Esto puso a Jesús en desacuerdo con el liderazgo del Templo. • Los evangelios sinópticos sitúan la limpieza del Templo cerca del final del ministerio de Jesús (Mat 21.12–13, Mar 11.15–17, Lc 19.45–46). Juan podría haber colocado su relato del evento aquí para enfatizar una conexión con el milagro que transformó en vino el agua en las jarras de purificación (Juan 2.1–11). El Templo y las jarras de piedra eran ambos instrumentos de purificación en el judaísmo. Las jarras de piedra llenas de agua para el lavado ritual ahora contenían el vino de Jesús, y un Templo de piedra dedicado a la purificación sacrificial sería reemplazado por el proprio Cristo (2.19–21). Otra visión es que Jesús limpió el Templo al principio y nuevamente al final de su ministerio.

text_src:
⸢Destroy this temple⸣: Herod the Great started rebuilding the temple's grand structure in 20 BC. The work continued until AD 64. This is why Jesus amazed his audience when he claimed he could destroy and rebuild it in a few days. 

However, Jesus was speaking figuratively (using a word picture) about his own body. He described his body as the true temple, the place where God was present (see 1:14, 51). 

His body would be destroyed. Three days later, God would raise him from the dead. Through his resurrection, Jesus showed that he himself was now the true place where people meet God. Because of this, the Jerusalem Temple and its sacrifices were no longer necessary.

Later, during the trial of Jesus, some people misunderstood his words. They used his statement about destroying the temple as evidence against him. They accused him of blasphemy (Mark 14:58).
text_es_aquifer: "Destruir este templo": Herodes el Grande comenzó a reconstruir la magnífica estructura del Templo en el año 20 a.C., y el trabajo continuó hasta el año 64 d.C. Esto explica por qué la audiencia de Jesús se asombró cuando afirmó que podía destruirlo y reconstruirlo en unos pocos días. Sin embargo, Jesús hablaba figurativamente de su propio cuerpo como el templo donde Dios estaba presente (ver 1.14, 51); su cuerpo fue destruido y restaurado en tres días a través de la resurrección, haciendo obsoleto el Templo de Jerusalén y sus servicios. Más tarde, en su juicio, la referencia simbólica de Jesús a la destrucción el Templo fue utilizada como prueba de blasfemia (Marcos 14.58).

text_src: ⸢they believed⸣: Seeing a miracle from God can lead people to believe. However, this kind of belief is not the deepest faith. The deepest faith trusts Jesus even without seeing miracles (20:29).
text_es_aquifer: "ellos creyeron": Presenciar un milagro de Dios puede inspirar creencia, pero no es la fe más profunda posible (20.29).

text_src:
John uses a play on words here. Because of Jesus’s signs (miracles that show who he is), many people trusted in him (2:23). But Jesus did not trust them in the same way.

This statement does not refer only to certain people in Jerusalem. It shows that Jesus knows what is inside every person. He understands people’s thoughts, motives (reasons for acting), and desires.
text_es_aquifer: Juan usa un juego de palabras aquí. Debido a sus señales, muchas personas creyeron en Jesús (2.23), pero Jesús no confiaba en ellos. Esto no se refería a personas específicas que Jesús conoció en Jerusalén, sino que refleja su conocimiento de toda la humanidad.

text_src:
John connects 2:25 and 3:1 by using the same Greek word (⸢anthrōpos⸣) to refer to all of humanity and then to a specific man (Nicodemus). Nicodemus had deep religious knowledge. He had also seen what Jesus was doing in Jerusalem (2:13–24). But he had not yet experienced spiritual rebirth (a new life that comes from God).⸢A Pharisee⸣: See study note on 1:24. The Pharisees were a Jewish group who were careful to obey the law of Moses and their religious traditions.

Nicodemus belonged to this group. He was part of the religious leaders. He was respected for his knowledge of the Jewish law. He likely took pride in his careful obedience and moral purity.
text_es_aquifer: Juan vincula 2.25 y 3.1 al referise a la humanidad en su conjunto (“naturaleza humana,” 2.25) y luego a un hombre específico usando la misma palabra griega (⸢anthrōpos⸣) en ambos versículos. • Nicodemo estaba lleno de conocimiento religioso y había presenciado la obra de Jesús (2.13–24), pero no había experimentado el renacimiento espiritual. • "un fariseo": ver nota de estudio en 1.24. Pertenecía a la élite, orgulloso de su pureza espiritual y bien instruido en la ley judía.

text_src: ⸢at night⸣: Nicodemus might have been afraid for others to see him with Jesus. In the Gospel of John, ⸢night⸣ often has a deeper meaning. It can represent evil, error (wrong belief), and unbelief (lack of trust in God; see 9:4; 11:10; 13:30).
text_es_aquifer: "Después del anochecer": Nicodemo podría haber temido la asociación pública con Jesús. La noche también simboliza el reino del mal, la falsedad y la incredulidad (9.4, 11.10, 13.30).

text_src:
⸢Born again: ⸣To experience spiritual birth, God's power must completely renew a person. Nicodemus thought Jesus was speaking about physical birth. He demonstrated that those in darkness, who do not have spiritual rebirth, cannot understand Jesus or other “heavenly things” (3:12). 

Jesus sometimes used ironic misunderstanding as a way to teach. He would say something with a deeper spiritual meaning. The listener would misunderstand his words in a simple or physical way. Then Jesus would explain the deeper meaning.

This method helped people see the difference between earthly thinking and spiritual truth.
text_es_aquifer: "nacer de nuevo": o "nacer de arriba"⸢.⸣ La expresión de Juan “de arriba” (3.31, 19.11) significa “de Dios.” Para experimentar el renacimiento espiritual, una persona debe ser completamente renovada a través del poder de Dios. • Nicodemo interpretó literalmente las palabras de Jesús; con ello demostró que los que están en las tinieblas, que no han renacido espiritualmente, no pueden entender a Jesús ni otras "cosas celestiales" (3.12). Jesús a veces usaba el malentendido irónico como una estrategia de enseñanza.

text_src: John the Baptist baptized with water⸢. ⸣Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33).
text_es_aquifer: Juan el Bautista bautizó con agua⸢,⸣ Jesús bautiza con el Espíritu (1.33).

text_src: In Greek, the word for ⸢wind⸣ is the same as for ⸢spirit⸣ (Greek ⸢pneuma⸣). The wind is an appropriate image for the Spirit⸢,⸣ who is sent from heaven and cannot be contained or controlled.
text_es_aquifer: La palabra utilizada para traducir "viento" es la misma que se utiliza en griego para traducir "espíritu" (⸢pneuma⸣). El viento es una imagen adecuada para el Espíritu⸢,⸣ que es enviado del cielo y no puede ser contenido ni controlado.

text_src:
There is a great distance between this world and heaven (see 1:51; 3:31; 6:38, 42). Heaven represents God’s dwelling place. This world represents human life under sin and weakness.

Jesus came down from heaven to this world. He made a way for people to know God. He proved that he came from God when he defeated death. After rising from the dead, he returned to the Father in heaven (16:5–11).
text_es_aquifer: Hay una gran distancia entre este mundo y el cielo (ver 1.51, 3.31, 6.38, 42). Jesús superó esa distancia, validando su estatus divino al vencer la muerte y regresar al cielo (16.5–11).

text_src: Jesus was lifted up on the cross so that all people could understand the way of salvation, look to him in faith, and have eternal life.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús fue levantado en la cruz para que todas las personas pudieran entender el camino de la salvación, mirarlo con fe y tener vida eterna.

text_src: The truth that God loved the world is basic to Christian understanding (1 John 4:9–10). God's love extends beyond the limits of race and nation, even to those who oppose him (see “The World” Theme Note). The Son came to save, not to condemn, people who often choose spiritual darkness (3:17, 19–21).
text_es_aquifer: La verdad de que Dios amó al mundo es fundamental para la comprensión cristiana (1 Jn 4.9–10). El amor de Dios se extiende más allá de los límites de raza y nación, incluso a aquellos que se oponen a él (ver Nota Temática “El Mundo”). • El Hijo vino a salvar, no a condenar (3.17), a hombres y mujeres que habitualmente abrazan las tinieblas (3.19–21).

text_src: The original Greek text does not include quotation marks. Because of this, translators must decide where the words of Jesus end and where John's explanation begins. John 3:16–21 might be John’s explanation of what Jesus said.
text_es_aquifer: Como en el texto griego no hay comillas alrededor del discurso de Jesús, los traductores debaten dónde termina el discurso de Jesús y dónde empieza el comentario de Juan; 3.16–21 podría ser el comentario de Juan.

text_src:
As light shines into a dark place, it reveals what was hidden. In the same way, when Jesus came into the world, he exposed its sin and unbelief. Because of this, God’s judgment has already begun.

People who see this light and understand their true condition must respond. They are responsible to believe in God’s Son (3:16–17).
text_es_aquifer: A medida que la luz penetra y expone las tinieblas del mundo, el juicio de Dios sobre el mundo ya ha comenzado. Los que ven esta luz y reconocen la tragedia de su propia situación tienen la responsabilidad de creer en el Hijo de Dios (3.16–17).

text_src:
When people live in spiritual darkness (a life separated from God), they do not want the light that Jesus brings. Jesus called himself "the light of the world" (8:12; 9:5). His light shows truth and exposes sin.

Darkness does not simply ignore the light. It resists it and tries to overcome it. But the darkness cannot defeat the light (1:5). 

Those who refuse to believe continue to live in darkness (13:30). They stumble because they cannot see clearly (11:10). In the end, their sins will be revealed. God will judge all people (5:28–30; Revelation 20:11–15).
text_es_aquifer: Cuando las personas viven en tinieblas espirituales, no desean ser iluminadas por Jesús, “la luz del mundo” (8.12; 9.5). El mal y las tinieblas no ignoran la luz, sino que le hacen la guerra, tratando de derribarla. Pero la oscuridad no puede apagar la luz (1.5). Los que se niegan a creer viven en la oscuridad (cf. 13.30) y tropiezan porque no pueden ver (11.10). Al final, sin embargo, sus pecados serán expuestos (5.28–30, Ap 20.11–15).

text_src: ⸢He spent some time with them and baptized⸣: See John 4:2, which explains that the disciples of Jesus were the ones who baptized people.
text_es_aquifer: "Jesús pasó algún tiempo . . . bautizando": ver 4:2, que aclara que los discípulos de Jesús fueron los que bautizaron.

text_src: John the Baptist says Jesus is truly "from above" (3:31). So, the followers of John need to start following Jesus instead.
text_es_aquifer: Juan el Bautista identifica a Jesús como el que verdaderamente viene de lo alto (3.31); esto requiere que los seguidores de Juan cambien su lealtad a Jesús.

text_src:
Before King Herod imprisoned John (see Matthew 14:1–12; Mark 1:14; 6:14–29; Luke 3:19–20), he and Jesus were both ministering near the Jordan River. They were working in the same general area.

After John was arrested, Jesus left that region. He traveled north to Galilee and began his ministry there (Mark 1:14).
text_es_aquifer: Antes de que Juan fuera encarcelado (ver Mt 14.1–12, Mc 1.14, 6.14–29, Lc 3.19–20), él y Jesús trabajaban muy cerca del río Jordán. Una vez que Juan fue aprisionado, Jesús se trasladó al norte, a Galilea (Mc 1.14).

text_src: ⸢everyone is going to Him⸣: Many people were going to Jesus. His growing popularity made some of John’s followers jealous.
text_es_aquifer: "todos vienen a él": la popularidad de Jesús provocó la envidia de algunos seguidores de Juan.

text_src: John the Baptist spoke because of two concerns: Some people questioned whether his baptism was from God (see 1:26), andhis disciples were worried because many people were beginning to follow Jesus instead of John (3:26).
text_es_aquifer: El discurso de Juan el Bautista fue inspirado por dos cuestiones: (1) algunos habían cuestionado la legitimidad de su bautismo (ver 1.26), y (2) sus discípulos estaban preocupados porque la gente comenzaba a seguir a Jesús en lugar de a Juan (3.26).

text_src:
John the Baptist described Jesus as the bridegroom. He described himself as the bridegroom’s friend.

John did not try to bring honor to himself. Instead, he gave honor to Jesus and showed that Jesus is greater than he is.
text_es_aquifer: Juan el Bautista vio a Jesús como el novio y a sí mismo como el amigo del novio. Su respuesta desvió la gloria de sí mismo y elevó la importancia de Jesús.

text_src: Jesus came from heaven. Because of this, he alone was able to make the Father known (1:18; 3:13).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús había venido del cielo⸢,⸣ por lo que era el único capaz de revelar al Padre (1.18, 3.13).

text_src: ⸢God gives the Spirit without limit⸣: The Father shows his deep love for the Son (3:35). This also shows the divine nature of Jesus. John presents the one God as three persons (compare 1 John 5:5–12).
text_es_aquifer: El Padre da al Hijo el Espíritu sin límites como signo de su profundo amor (3.35). También ilustra la divinidad de Jesús. Juan presenta al único Dios como tres personas (cf. 1 Jn 5.5–12).

text_src: God gives the gift of eternal life. This life is not only about the future. It begins now. It is a new life and a close relationship with God in the present.⸢Whoever rejects the Son will not see life⸣: The world, living in darkness and sin, already stands under God’s judgment (Romans 1–3). This judgment shows God’s anger against sin and evil.
text_es_aquifer: Dios dio el don de la vida eterna⸢,⸣ prometiendo nueva vida e intimidad en una experiencia presente con Dios. • Aquellos que rechazan al Hijo no verán la vida. El mundo en sus tinieblas permanece bajo la ira del juicio de Dios (Rm 1–3).

text_src:
At an ancient well in Samaria, Jesus offered himself as ⸢living water⸣. This ⸢living water⸣ means the life that comes from God. Jesus spoke openly about who he was. When he revealed God’s truth, people had to respond. They either followed him or turned away.The Samaritan woman is very different from Nicodemus. She was a woman, not a man. She was a Samaritan, not a Jew. She had a sinful past, not a reputation for righteousness. She was an outsider, not a respected teacher of Israel.

Nicodemus came to Jesus at night and did not openly respond to the challenges from Jesus (3:1–21). The Samaritan woman spoke with Jesus in the daylight. She recognized him as Lord. She remained in the light and showed signs of becoming a disciple (see 1:35–51).
text_es_aquifer: En un pozo histórico en Samaria, Jesús se ofreció como agua viva. Jesús se comprometía y confrontaba a la gente con la revelación de Dios, y ellos o le seguían o se alejaban. • La mujer samaritana contrastaba con Nicodemo en todo momento: una mujer (no un hombre), una samaritana (no un judío), una pecadora (no un justo) y un paria (no uno de los rabinos de Israel). Mientras Nicodemo permanecía en silencio y nunca respondía a las preguntas de Jesús (3.1–21), esta mujer reconoció a Jesús como Señor, permaneció en la luz y mostró signos de discipulado (ver 1.35–51).

text_src:
Jesus himself did not baptize anyone with water. He allowed his disciples to perform water baptism.

Later, after he was lifted up on the cross and then raised from the dead, Jesus returned to the Father. This suffering, death, resurrection, and return to the Father is called his glorification (7:37–39). After this, Jesus baptized people in the Holy Spirit (1:33; Acts 2:4).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús mismo no bautizó a nadie, sino que dejó el bautismo en agua a sus discípulos⸢.⸣ Después de su glorificación en la cruz (7.37–39), Jesús bautizó a las personas en el Espíritu Santo (1.33, Hechos 2.4).

text_src: After John the Baptist had been imprisoned, Jesus left Judea (see Mark 6:14–29; compare Mark 1:14).
text_es_aquifer: Después de que Juan el Bautista fue encarcelado (ver Marcos 6:14–29), Jesús dejó Judea (cf. Marcos 1:14).

text_src: When traveling north to Galilee, Jesus chose the less common route through Samaria. Samaria and Judea had a long history of racial tension (see 2 Kings 17:24–41; Ezra 4:1–5; Nehemiah 4; 6:1–19). In the time of Jesus, there was intense racial and cultural conflict between Jews and Samaritans. Jews usually avoided Samaria by first going east to Jericho and then traveling north through the Jordan Valley. Sychar was likely in the area of Shechem. Jesus arrived at Jacob's well. Jacob had owned land near Shechem (Genesis 33:18–19).
text_es_aquifer: Al ir al norte hacia Galilea, Jesús tomó la ruta menos preferida a través de Samaria. Samaria tenía una larga historia de tensión con Judea (ver 2 Re 17:24–41; Esd 4:1–5; Ne 4; 6;1–19). En los días de Jesús, existía un fuerte conflicto racial y cultural entre judíos y samaritanos. Los judíos normalmente evitaban Samaria yendo primero al este, hacia Jericó, y luego siguiendo el Valle del Jordán hacia el norte. • Sicar probablemente estaba en la región de Siquem. Jesús había llegado al pozo de Jacob⸢;⸣ Jacob había poseído tierras cerca de Siquem (Gn 33:18–19).

text_src: Due to the heat, it was customary for the women to draw water in early morning or evening. However, this woman lived in isolation, separated from her community. Jesus was compassionate toward outcasts.
text_es_aquifer: Debido al calor, era costumbre que las mujeres sacaran agua temprano en la mañana o en la tarde. Sin embargo, esta mujer vivía aislada, separada de su comunidad. Jesús era compasivo con los marginados.

text_src: The woman was surprised. Social taboos (strict cultural rules about proper behavior) would normally prevent a Jewish teacher like Jesus from speaking to her (4:18). But Jesus did not allow these social rules to control him. He chose to speak with her and offer what she truly needed.
text_es_aquifer: La mujer se sorprendió porque los tabúes sociales impedirían a un maestro judío como Jesús hablar con ella (4.18). Sin embargo, Jesús no dejó que los tabúes sociales le impidieran darle lo que ella realmente necesitaba.

text_src: Shechem had no rivers. So it had no ⸢living water,⸣ which usually means fresh, flowing water from a stream or spring (see “Living Water” Theme Note). However, Jesus was speaking symbolically. The gift he offered was not ordinary water. It was the Holy Spirit, whom God would give to believers (7:37–39).
text_es_aquifer: Siquem no tenía ríos y, por lo tanto, no tenía agua viva (ver Nota Temática “Agua Viva”). Sin embargo, Jesús hablaba simbólicamente: este don de Dios era el Espíritu Santo (7:37–39).

text_src:
Jacob’s well was more than 30 meters (about 100 feet) deep. A person needed a long rope and a container to draw water from it.

The woman focused on the physical water in the well. She did not yet understand the deeper meaning of what Jesus was saying. At that time, she was still in spiritual darkness.
text_es_aquifer: El pozo de Jacob tenía más de 30 metros de profundidad y requería una cuerda larga para sacar agua. La mujer malinterpretó las palabras de Jesús porque todavía estaba a oscuras.

text_src: ⸢Our father Jacob⸣: The Samaritan woman respected the holy traditions related to the well more than the presence of God in front of her.
text_es_aquifer: "nuestro padre Jacob": la mujer samaritana apeló con reverencia a las tradiciones sagradas vinculadas al pozo más que a la presencia de Dios ante ella.

text_src:
In the dry climate of Israel, a fresh, bubbling spring was a strong and hopeful image. Flowing water meant life, safety, and relief from thirst.

The prophets used this image to describe God’s care. They said that those who come to God will not hunger or thirst (see Isaiah 49:10; 55:1–3; Jeremiah 2:13).
text_es_aquifer: La noción de un manantial fresco y burbujeante era una imagen poderosa en el clima seco de Israel. Aquellos que vienen a Dios no tendrán hambre ni sed (ver Is 49:10, 55:1–3, Jr 2.13).

text_src: The woman asked Jesus for this water, but she did not understand the spiritual meaning of his words. To overcome this spiritual barrier, Jesus spoke about her sin (4:16–18).
text_es_aquifer: La mujer le pidió a Jesús esta agua, pero no entendió las implicaciones espirituales de las palabras que él le había dicho. Para superar la barrera espiritual, Jesús abordó su pecado (4:16–18).

text_src:
The woman’s immoral life affected her understanding. Her pattern of broken relationships kept her from seeing clearly.

She had been married five times. She was also living with a man who was not her husband. These facts show that her life did not match God’s will. Her sin created a barrier between her and a full understanding of what Jesus was saying.
text_es_aquifer: La inmoralidad bloqueó la comprensión de la mujer. Sus aventuras conyugales, incluido el haber tenido cinco maridos, subrayaron su vida pecaminosa.

text_src: ⸢a prophet⸣: Jesus revealed knowledge about the woman that a stranger could not know (4:16–18; compare 1:48). As the woman learned more about Jesus, what she called him showed her increasing understanding:At first, she recognized him as "a Jew" (4:9) and called him "Sir" (4:11, 15, 19). Later, she thought he might be "the Christ" (4:29), that is, the Messiah (God's chosen one). Finally, the people of the village recognized him as "the Savior of the world" (4:42). Her growing understanding of the identity of Jesus is a lesson for John’s audience (see 20:31).
text_es_aquifer: "un profeta": Jesús reveló conocimiento sobre la mujer (4:16–18) que era inaccesible para una persona normal (cf. 1:48). • A medida que la mujer fue entendiendo mejor a Jesús, los nombres que le daba se fueron haciendo cada vez más claros. Anteriormente lo reconoció como "un judío" (4.9) y lo llamó "señor" (4:11, 15, 19). Más tarde pensó que podría ser "el Mesías" (4.29). Finalmente, la gente del pueblo lo reconoció como "Salvador del mundo" (4:42). La creciente comprensión de la identidad de Jesús por parte de esta mujer es un testimonio para los lectores de Juan (ver 20:31).

text_src:
The woman did not answer the moral questions that Jesus asked her. Instead, she changed the subject.

She began to speak about the long-standing division between Jews and Samaritans. This conflict included differences about worship and history. By raising this issue, she moved the conversation away from her personal life.
text_es_aquifer: La mujer esquivó el sondeo moral de Jesús y mencionó la división étnica histórica entre judíos y samaritanos.

text_src:
The Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim. This mountain rises above the city of Shechem.

Both Mount Gerizim and Shechem were important places in the Old Testament (see Genesis 12:6–7; 33:19; Deuteronomy 11:29; Joshua 8:33; 24:1, 25, 32).
text_es_aquifer: Los samaritanos adoraban en el monte Gerizim, que se elevaba sobre Siquem.  Ambos eran lugares importantes del Antiguo Testamento (ver Gn 12:6–7, 33:19; Dt 11:29; Jos 8:33, 24:1, 25, 32).

text_src: Jesus affirmed that the Jews had preserved the correct understanding of the one true God whom they worshiped.God chose the Jewish people for a special relationship with himself. He gave them his law, his promises, and his covenant (promises between God and his people). The Messiah (God’s chosen one) was to come from the Jewish people (see also Romans 9:4–5).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús afirmó que los judíos habían preservado la correcta comprensión de Aquel a quién adoran. • "la salvación viene a través de los judíos": Dios dio a los judíos una relación especial con él, y el Mesías iba a ser judío (ver también Rm 9:4–5).

text_src:
⸢in spirit and in truth⸣: In Greek, one preposition (a connecting word) is used for both words. This shows that ⸢spirit and truth⸣ form one united idea.

True worship happens when God’s Spirit makes God’s truth known to a person. Worship is not only about a place or a ceremony. It is about responding to God with the help of his Spirit and according to what is true about him.

Jesus himself is the Truth (14:6). The Spirit is also called the Spirit of truth (14:17; 15:26). Together, the Spirit and the Truth make true worship possible.
text_es_aquifer: "en espíritu y en verdad": Una preposición griega rige ambas palabras (literalmente "en espíritu y verdad") y las convierte en un solo concepto. La verdadera adoración ocurre cuando el Espíritu de Dios revela la verdad y la realidad de Dios al adorador. Jesucristo es la Verdad (14:6, cp. 14:17, 15:26).

text_src:
⸢I who speak to you am He⸣: Jesus used an unusual and strong form of the words ⸢I am⸣.

This wording may point beyond a simple statement of identity. It can suggest a connection with the name of God revealed in the Old Testament (see 8:58; Exodus 3:14).
text_es_aquifer: "Soy yo el Mesías" (el griego dice "Soy yo, el que te habla"): La frase de Jesús era inusual y enfática, y sugiere identidad con Dios (ver 8:58, Ex 3:14).

text_src:
The woman was not fully certain about who Jesus was (4:29). She asked the people of her village, ⸢“Could this be the Christ?”⸣ Her words show that she was still thinking and learning.

Even so, she ran back to the village and told others about him. She invited them to come and see for themselves.

Telling others about Jesus is a sign of discipleship. Earlier in this Gospel, others also invited people to “come and see”(see 1:39, 46).
text_es_aquifer: La mujer estaba indecisa sobre la identidad de Jesús (4:29), sin embargo, corrió al pueblo y les dijo a todos que vinieran a verlo. Testificar a otros es una señal de discipulado (ver 1:39, 46).

text_src:
While Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman, the disciples had gone to buy food  (4:8). When they returned, they urged Jesus to eat. Jesus spoke with symbolic language, but they did not understand him (4:33). 

Later, when the disciples received the Holy Spirit, they understood what he meant (2:22). Jesus sustained himself spiritually by doing what his Father told him to do (see 5:30; 6:38; 7:18; 8:50; 9:4; 10:37–38; 12:49–50).
text_es_aquifer: Mientras Jesús hablaba con la mujer samaritana, los discípulos habían ido a comprar comida (4:8); ahora instaron a Jesús a comer. Jesús continuó hablando simbólicamente, pero ellos no lo entendieron (4:33). Más tarde, cuando los discípulos recibieron el Espíritu, entendieron (2:22). Jesús recibía su alimento al hacer lo que su Padre le decía que hacer (ver 5:30, 6:38, 7:18, 8:50, 9:4, 10:37–38, 12:49–50).

text_src:
⸢four months until the harvest⸣: Jesus referred to a common saying about farming. Farmers usually waited about four months between planting seed and gathering the crop.

In Samaria, it was likely the time of harvest, and the fields were ready to be gathered. Jesus used this picture to speak about people, not crops.

He had spoken with the woman at the well and planted spiritual seed (God’s message). Soon after, many Samaritans believed in him (4:39–42). In this way, Jesus was already gathering a harvest of faith.
text_es_aquifer: "Cuatro meses entre la siembra y la cosecha": Jesús citó una parábola local para contrastar la cosecha natural con la suya. Era tiempo de cosecha en Samaria, y los campos estaban maduros. Jesús, sin embargo, había sembrado semillas junto al pozo y ahora ya estaba recogiendo la cosecha de la fe entre los samaritanos (4:39–42).

text_src: ⸢others⸣: Jesus might have meant John the Baptist. Or, he might have been referring to the work he had just done with the Samaritan woman.
text_es_aquifer: "otros": Jesús podría haberse referido a Juan el Bautista, o al trabajo que acababa de hacer con la mujer samaritana.

text_src: ⸢Many of the Samaritans⸣: The religious leaders and teachers in Jerusalem did not respond to Jesus with faith (chapter 3). In contrast, many Samaritans believed in him. They first listened because of the testimony (public witness) of this woman, who had been an outsider in her community. Later, they believed because they heard Jesus for themselves.
text_es_aquifer: "Muchos samaritanos": El religiosamente sofisticado "pueblo elegido" en Jerusalén no respondió a Jesús con fe (cap. 3). En cambio, muchos samaritanos creyeron en Jesús por el testimonio de esta mujer marginada.

text_src:
The Samaritans had heard Jesus and believed his message for themselves. They were no longer depending only on the woman’s testimony.

They called him ⸢Savior of the world⸣ (see also 1 John 4:14). This title shows that they understood something important. Salvation was not limited to one ethnic group.

As Samaritans, they knew they were separated from the Jews. Yet they recognized that Jesus came for all people. His mission was not only for Jews, but for the whole world (John 1:4–12; compare 12:20–26).
text_es_aquifer: Los samaritanos habían experimentado por sí mismos que Jesús era verdadero. Su nombre para Jesús, Salvador del mundo (también usado en 1 Jn 4:14), demostraba que los samaritanos eran muy conscientes de su distancia del judaísmo. El ministerio de Jesús no era simplemente para los judíos, sino para todas las personas (Jn 1:4–12, cp. 12:20–26).

text_src:
Unlike many people in Jerusalem, the Galileans welcomed Jesus when he came to them.

However, their welcome was based on amazement at his miracles (see 2:23–25). They were impressed by what he did.

This response was not yet true faith. True faith trusts in who Jesus is, not only in the signs and wonders he performs.
text_es_aquifer: A diferencia de los otros compatriotas judíos de Jesús, los galileos le dieron la bienvenida, pero su bienllegada se basó en el asombro ante los milagros de Jesús (cp. 2:23–25), no en la verdadera fe.

text_src: Jesus strongly criticized the Galileans for asking to see miracles and wonders before they would believe (see 6:30).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús criticó duramente a los galileos que deseaban señales y maravillas milagrosas antes de creer (ver 6:30).

text_src: ⸢"Your son will live"⸣: Jesus also healed the centurion’s servant and the Phoenician woman’s daughter from a distance (Matthew 8:5–13; 15:21–28).
text_es_aquifer: "¡Tu hijo vivirá!" Jesús también sanó al esclavo del centurión (Mt 8:5–13) y a la hija de la mujer fenicia (Mt 15:21–28) desde lejos.

text_src: Like many other people, the Jewish official and his household believed in Jesus because of the miracle (2:23; 4:39).
text_es_aquifer: Como muchos otros (2:23, 4:39), el oficial y su casa creyeron en Jesús a causa del milagro.

text_src: ⸢the second sign …⸣⸢ in Galilee⸣: Two miracles at Cana frame for this section of John's Gospel (2:11; 4:46). The first miracle was when Jesus turned water into wine. The second was when he healed the official’s son. These two events mark the beginning and the end of this part of the story.
text_es_aquifer: "segunda señal milagrosa . . . en Galilea": dos milagros en Caná (2:11, 4:46) enmarcan esta sección del Evangelio de Juan.

text_src:
⸢a feast of the Jews⸣: Jesus returned to Jerusalem for this celebration. Because of this, it was likely one of the three main pilgrimage festivals (special festivals when people traveled to Jerusalem).

In the Old Testament, God commanded Israel to celebrate three such festivals each year (see Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16). These were the Feast of Unleavened Bread (also called Passover), the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles.

Each of these festivals lasted about one week. During that time, many people gathered in Jerusalem to worship God.
text_es_aquifer: "una de las fiestas judías": Como Jesús regresó a Jerusalén para la celebración, probablemente se trataba de una de las tres fiestas de peregrinación del judaísmo (ver Ex 23:14–17, Dt 16:16). Estos festivales duraban una semana.

text_src: This chapter is structured like a courtroom case (a legal trial). It begins with a description of the event that led to the conflict (5:1–15). This is followed by the decision of the Jewish leaders to take action against Jesus (5:16). Next comes a statement of the charges against him (5:18). The chapter then presents the defense given by Jesus, where he explains his authority and his relationship with the Father (5:17, 19–40).
text_es_aquifer: Este capítulo se lee como un drama judicial, con una descripción del crimen (5.1–15), seguida de una decisión de enjuiciar (5.16), una descripción de las acusaciones (5.18), y la defensa de Jesús (5.17, 19–40).

text_src:
In this section, Jesus attends several Jewish feasts and uses their imagery to reveal deeper truths about himself. 

He appears at:a Sabbath feast (chapter 5),Passover (chapter 6),the Feast of Tabernacles (chapters 7–9), andthe Feast of Dedication (also called Hanukkah; chapter 10). In each case, Jesus himself replaces an important element in the ceremonies of the feast.
text_es_aquifer: En esta sección, Jesús aparece en una serie de festivales judíos y utiliza el simbolismo religioso para revelar verdades más profundas sobre sí mismo. Aparece en un sábado (cap. 5), en la Pascua (cap. 6), en el Festival de los Tabernáculos (caps. 7–9) y en el  Hanukkah (cap. 10). En cada caso, Jesús es el sustituto de algún elemento vital en las ceremonias festivas.

text_src: Greek copyists who had never been to Jerusalem had difficulty interpreting and spelling the name Bethesda⸢,⸣ so there are several variants of this name in the manuscripts. The best choice is ⸢Beth-esda⸣, which means “house of flowing.”
text_es_aquifer: Los copistas griegos que nunca habían estado en Jerusalén tuvieron dificultades para interpretar y deletrear el nombre Betesda⸢,⸣ por lo que existen diversas variantes de este nombre en los manuscritos. La mejor opción es ⸢Beth-esda⸣ (“casa de fluir”).

text_src: The pool of Bethesda was a place for healing where many sick people gathered. They hoped God would cure them with a miracle. Some later manuscripts include an additional verse, John 5:4, which explains that an angel stirred the water. This verse is not included in the Berean Standard Bible because it does not appear in the earliest manuscripts of the Gospel of John. The added verse reflects an early tradition that helps explain why people gathered at the pool.
text_es_aquifer: El estanque de Bethesda se había convertido en un santuario curativo para multitudes de personas enfermas que creían que las curas milagrosas eran posibles. • La mayoría de los eruditos creen que la lectura variante en la nota textual de la NTV no era parte del texto original de Juan, pero representa una antigua tradición que proporcionaba información de fondo útil.

text_src:
No organized care system existed to help this man. He had been sick for 38 years.

He likely could not keep himself clean. He probably could not move easily on his own. Most likely, he depended on begging from people who came to the pool (see 5:7). From a human point of view, his situation seemed hopeless.
text_es_aquifer: Ningún programa social ayudó a este hombre, que llevaba treinta y ocho años enfermo. La higiene y la movilidad eran imposibles, y probablemente, para vivir, mendigaba de las personas que venían a usar la piscina (ver 5:7). Su situación parecía irremediable.

text_src:
Jesus healed the sick man immediately and only asked him to obey. To prove that the man was healed, Jesus told him to pick up his mat and walk.Jesus performed this miracle on the Sabbath. The Sabbath was a weekly day of rest. The law of Moses said that no work should be done on that day (based on Genesis 2:2; Exodus 20:8). Jewish tradition identified 39 types of work that were not allowed (⸢Mishnah Shabbat⸣ 7:2). One rule said that a person could not carry an object, such as a sleeping mat, from one place to another (John 5:10). 

Jesus told the healed man to pick up his mat and walk. When the man obeyed Jesus, he broke this later Jewish tradition.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús sanó al hombre enfermo instantáneamente⸢,⸣ solo pidiendo su obediencia. Como prueba de la curación, Jesús le dijo que recogiera su estera y caminara. • Jesús realizó este milagro en el Sabbath⸢,⸣ un día de descanso en la semana semana, en la cual se prohibía todo trabajo (basado en Gn 2:2, Ex 20:8). La tradición judía delineaba treinta y nueve categorías de trabajo que no estaban permitidas (⸢Mishnah⸣ ⸢Shabbat⸣ 7:2). Llevar algo como una estera de dormir de un lugar a otro estaba prohibido (Jn 5:10). Por lo tanto, el hombre sanado rompió la tradición al obedecer el mandato de Jesús.

text_src:
⸢Who is this man who told you⸣: The focus of the story now changes. It moves from the joy of a miracle to an accusation about breaking the Sabbath.

The religious leaders wanted to know who told the man to carry his mat. They asked for the name of the healer who had broken their tradition.
text_es_aquifer: "¿Quién dijo tal cosa?" La trama da un giro siniestro, pasando de un milagro maravilloso a un crimen cometido en sábado, que culmina con la petición de la identidad del sanador que violó la tradición.

text_src: ⸢Stop sinning⸣: Although Jesus healed this man physically, the man still needed to learn to obey the Lord. The man's next action (5:15) might indicate that he did not listen.
text_es_aquifer: "no peques más": Aunque el hombre había sido sanado físicamente, todavía necesitaba aprender a obedecer al Señor. La siguiente acción del hombre (5:15) podría indicar que no escuchó.

text_src:
⸢My Father is at His work, and I too am working⸣: The Sabbath was a day of rest. People were not supposed to work.

However, Jewish teachers agreed that God still worked on the Sabbath. God gives life through birth. God also takes life in death. God’s work does not stop.

Jesus used this idea to explain his actions. He said that, like his Father, he was also working. By speaking this way, Jesus compared himself with God.

The Jewish leaders understood what he meant. They objected because they believed he was claiming a special right that belongs only to God.
text_es_aquifer: "Mi Padre hasta ahora trabaja, y yo trabajo": Aunque el trabajo estaba prohibido en el sábados, incluso los rabinos estaban de acuerdo en que Dios trabajaba en el sábado dando vida (nacimientos) y quitando vida (muertes). El núcleo de la defensa de Jesús fue compararse con Dios; los dirigentes judíos se opusieron a esta afirmación de privilegio divino.

text_src: Jesus claimed that his work on the Sabbath was the same as God’s work on the Sabbath. Jesus claimed to be equal with God, doing the things God does. Yet he submitted to God’s will, doing only what the Father wanted.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús afirmó que su trabajo en el sábado era el mismo que el trabajo de Dios en el sábado. Jesús afirmó ser igual a Dios, haciendo las cosas que Dios hace. Sin embargo, se sometió a la voluntad de Dios, haciendo sólo lo que . . . el Padre quería.

text_src: Most Jews firmly believed in resurrection but viewed it as something God alone could accomplish. Jesus claimed that he gives life.
text_es_aquifer: La mayoría de los judíos creían firmemente en la resurrección, pero la consideraban como algo que solo Dios podía hacer. Jesús afirmó que él da vida.

text_src: In addition to giving life, Jesus claimed the absolute authority to judge⸢,⸣ which belongs to God alone.
text_es_aquifer: Además de dar vida, Jesús afirmó la autoridad absoluta para juzgar⸢,⸣ que pertenece solo a Dios.

text_src: ⸢the Father who sent Him⸣: In the ancient world, a person could send an authorized representative to seal a contract or make an authoritative decision. Jesus claimed to be God’s representative, so obeying Jesus is the same as obeying God, and dishonoring him is dishonoring God.
text_es_aquifer: "el Padre . . . lo envió": En el mundo antiguo, una persona podía enviar a un representante autorizado para sellar un contrato o tomar una decisión con autoridad. Jesús afirmó ser el representante de Dios, así que obedecer a Jesús es lo mismo que obedecer a Dios, y deshonrarlo es deshonrar a Dios.

text_src: Jesus is the giver of life as well as the judge (see 5:21–22), but he never works independently of the Father.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús es el dador de vida así como el juez (ver 5:21–22), pero nunca trabaja independientemente del Padre.

text_src:
God's law requires more than one witness in a trial (Deuteronomy 17:6). A single person’s word is not enough to prove a case.

Jesus recognized this principle. He said that his own testimony needed support from others.

So he presented several witnesses who confirmed who he was. These witnesses supported his claims and showed that his message was true.
text_es_aquifer: La ley de Dios requiere más de un testigo en un juicio (Dt 17:6), por lo que Jesús reconoció que su propio testimonio era admisible solo cuando era confirmado por otros testigos. Así, presentó una serie de testigos para su defensa.

text_src:
The first witness who spoke in support of Jesus was God himself.

Jesus may have been thinking about the voice from heaven at his baptism, when God said that Jesus was his Son (Mark 1:11). He may also have meant the power of God that worked through him in his miracles.

In both ways, God gave testimony about who Jesus is.
text_es_aquifer: El primer testigo de la defensa de Jesús fue Dios mismo. Jesús podría haber tenido en mente la voz de Dios en su bautismo (Marcos 1:11) o la presencia de Dios que permitió a Jesús realizar milagros.

text_src: The second witness of Jesus was John the Baptist. John pointed to Jesus and said that he is the Messiah (1:29–34).
text_es_aquifer: El segundo testigo de Jesús fue Juan el Bautista⸢,⸣ quien señaló a Jesús como el Mesías (1:29–34).

text_src: The third witness of Jesus was his teachings and miracles. These were signs that revealed his true identity and indicated that the Father sent him.
text_es_aquifer: El tercer testimonio de Jesús, sus enseñanzas y milagros, eran signos que desvelaban su verdadera identidad y señalaban al Padre que lo había enviado.

text_src: The fourth witness of Jesus was the Scriptures. The Old Testament pointed to the Messiah, and Jesus fulfilled its prophecies (see Luke 24:25–27).
text_es_aquifer: El cuarto testigo de Jesús fueron las Escrituras. El Antiguo Testamento señalaba al Mesías, y Jesús cumplió sus profecías (ver Lucas 24:25–27).

text_src:
Jewish trials were meant to discover the truth. The goal was to decide whether the charges were true or false.

If people were falsely accused, they could show that they were innocent. He could also bring charges against those who had accused him. In this situation, Jesus did that.
text_es_aquifer: Los juicios judíos buscaban descubrir la verdad. Los acusados falsamente no solo podían probar su inocencia sino también procesar a sus acusadores, lo cual Jesús hizo aquí.

text_src:
Jesus said that the Jewish leaders did not have God’s love in them. They did not truly love God.

Because they did not love God, they could not understand what Jesus was doing. Without love for God, they were unable to recognize God’s work in him.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús acusó a los líderes judíos de no tener el amor de Dios dentro de ellos. Sin el amor de Dios, les era imposible entender las cosas que él estaba haciendo.

text_src:
The Jewish leaders wanted honor and praise from one another. They cared about their reputation and status.

They loved religious activity, but they did not truly love God. Their actions did not match their claims. Because of this, God would judge them (5:45–46).
text_es_aquifer: Los líderes judíos buscaban honor y prestigio entre ellos. Amaban la vida religiosa, pero se habían olvidado de amar a Dios. Esta hipocresía los hacía responsables del juicio (5:45–46).

text_src: The fifth and final witness for Jesus was Moses, the central figure through whom God gave the law to Israel. Earlier in the Gospel of John, Jesus is compared with Moses, who gave the law, while Jesus brought grace and truth (1:17; see also 6:14–15). The Jewish leaders failed to accept the words of Moses, who spoke clearly about the coming Messiah, including the promise of a prophet like himself (for example, Deuteronomy 18:15).
text_es_aquifer: El quinto y último testigo de Jesús fue Moisés⸢,⸣ el padre fundador del judaísmo. Juan ya había comparado a Jesús con Moisés (1:17, ver también 6:14–15). Los líderes judíos estaban ignorando las claras palabras de Moisés sobre el Mesías (por ejemplo, Dt 18:15).

text_src:
Jesus feeding the 5,000 recalls the Old Testament story of manna (bread from heaven) when Israel was in the wilderness (Exodus 16). In that story, God provided bread each day for his people.

In the time of Jesus, some Jewish teachers believed that the Messiah would again give bread from heaven (Exodus 16:4). They expected a new act of divine provision.

When Jesus fed the crowd, he met this expectation. However, he was not only giving physical bread. He was pointing to himself as the true bread from heaven, who gives life to the world.
text_es_aquifer: La alimentación de los 5,000 por Jesús recuerda el gran milagro del Antiguo Testamento del pan cuando Israel estaba en el desierto (Éxodo 16). Los rabinos del tiempo de Jesús esperaban que el Mesías venidero “hiciera llover comida del cielo” una vez más (Éxodo 16:4), y lo hizo.

text_src: Each story in this chapter uses the setting of the Feast of the Passover (6:4) to communicate a deeper meaning.
text_es_aquifer: Cada historia en este capítulo utiliza el escenario del Festival de la Pascua (6:4) para comunicar un significado más profundo.

text_src: ⸢Where can we buy bread⸣: When the Israelites left Egypt after the first Passover and entered the desert, finding food and water was also their first concern (Exodus 15:22–16:3).
text_es_aquifer: "¿Dónde podemos comprar pan?": Cuando los israelitas salieron de Egipto después de la primera Pascua y entraron en el desierto, encontrar comida y agua también fue su primera preocupación (Éxodo 15:22–16:3).

text_src: Barley was a grain for poor people. The loaves were like pita bread. The two fish were likely salted. Together with the five barley loaves, they made one meal.
text_es_aquifer: La cebada era el grano de los pobres. Los panes eran similares al pan de pita. Los dos peces habrían sido salados, y con los cinco panes de cebada harían una comida.

text_src: The count of about 5,000 included only the men, as was the usual way of counting in that culture (Matthew 14:21). Including women and children, the total number of people was much greater.
text_es_aquifer: El recuento de aproximadamente cinco mil reflejaba solo a los hombres (Mateo: 14–21), como dictaba la costumbre social. Con mujeres y niños incluidos, el número total era mucho mayor.

text_src: The simple meal provided the crowd with as much as they wanted. This was similar to the miracle of manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35). In that earlier story, God gave bread from heaven through Moses. Now, Jesus provided bread for the people in a similar way.
text_es_aquifer: La modesta comida proporcionó a la multitud tanto como querían, recordando la provisión milagrosa de maná en el desierto (Éxodo 16:35). Moisés había suministrado primero a Israel el pan celestial; Jesús era el nuevo proveedor.

text_src: ⸢Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world⸣: The crowd understood the miracle as a fulfillment of Old Testament promises (see Deuteronomy 18:15, 18; Malachi 4:5–6).
text_es_aquifer: "¡Él es el Profeta que hemos estado esperando!" La multitud entendió el milagro como un cumplimiento de las promesas del Antiguo Testamento (ver Dt 18:15-18, Ml 4:5–6).

text_src: ⸢they were about to come and make Him king by force⸣: To avoid this role, Jesus fled the crowd and commanded his disciples to go back across the lake (Mark 6:45–46).
text_es_aquifer: La gente estaba lista para forzar a Jesús a convertirse en su rey. Para evitar este papel, Jesús huyó de la multitud y ordenó a sus discípulos que regresaran al otro lado del lago (Marcos 6:45–46).

text_src:
Strong east-west winds often blow down from the eastern cliffs of the Sea of Galilee. These winds usually come late in the day.

When the wind rushes down toward the water, it can quickly stir up high waves. As a result, the lake can become very rough and dangerous. Sudden and violent storms were common in that area.
text_es_aquifer: Los vientos de este a oeste que soplan sobre los acantilados orientales del Mar de Galilea al final del día comúnmente causaban aguas muy agitadas y tormentas turbulentas.

text_src:
The disciples were afraid of the storm. Then they saw Jesus walking on the water toward them. At that moment, their fear of the storm was replaced by fear and awe of him. Jesus came to help them. By walking on the water, he showed his authority over nature.

This act recalled Moses, who led Israel safely through the water (Exodus 14; see Psalm 77:19–20).
text_es_aquifer: El miedo de los discípulos a la tormenta fue ahora superado por su miedo a Jesús⸢,⸣ quien vino caminando sobre el agua para ayudarlos. Este acto recordó a Moisés, quien condujo a Israel a través del agua (Éxodo 14, ver Salmo 77:19–20).

text_src: ⸢It is I⸣ (literally, ⸢I am⸣): Jesus identified himself by the name God had revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (see Exodus 3:14; also see John 4:26; 6:35).
text_es_aquifer: "Estoy aquí (el griego dice "Yo soy")": Jesús se identificó con el nombre que Dios había revelado a Moisés en el Monte Sinaí (ver Éxodo 3:14, ver también Juan 4:26, 6:35).
