text_src: ⸢at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading⸣: The healing happened at once. This immediate result was another miracle performed by Jesus.
text_es_aquifer: "inmediatamente llegaron a su destino": La inmediatez fue otro de los milagros de Jesús.

text_src: The crowd sailed north to Capernaum to search for Jesus because he had made Capernaum his home in Galilee (Mark 2:1).
text_es_aquifer: La multitud navegó hacia el norte a Capernaum para buscar a Jesús porque había hecho de Capernaum su hogar en Galilea (Marcos 2:1).

text_src:
The crowd had decided that Jesus was a prophet. They even wanted to use him for their own political goals (see 6:15). 

However, they did not understand the true meaning of the miracle. They focused on the bread and the signs.

Jesus then explained what the miracle really meant. He taught that people should not work only for food that spoils. Instead, they should seek the food that gives eternal life (6:27–59).
text_es_aquifer: La multitud, que había concluido que Jesús era un profeta y quería aprovecharse de él políticamente (ver 6:15), no logró ver el significado del milagro, que Jesús luego explicó (6:27–59).

text_src: This dialogue took place in the synagogue at Capernaum shortly before Passover (6:4, 59). During Passover, Jews would read the story of the exodus from Egypt (see Exodus 1–15).
text_es_aquifer: Este diálogo tuvo lugar en la sinagoga de Capernaum (6:59) poco antes de la Pascua (6:4), cuando los judíos leen el relato del éxodo de Egipto (ver Éxodo 1–15).

text_src:
The greatest gift Jesus gives is not physical bread, but eternal life. The Father gave Jesus the authority to do this. 

Physical food spoils. But Jesus, who is the bread of life, offers a gift that lasts forever (6:35).
text_es_aquifer: El regalo más profundo de Jesús no fue el pan físico, sino la vida eterna, que el Padre le autorizó a dar. El pan físico es perecedero⸢;⸣ el regalo de Jesús, quien es él mismo el pan de vida (6:35), durará para siempre.

text_src:
The crowd asked Jesus for another miraculous sign. They wanted proof that he was the Messiah.

Many Jews believed that when the Messiah came, he would repeat the great miracle connected with Moses. They expected manna to fall from heaven again, as it had in the wilderness.

If that happened, people would see it as a second exodus. It would remind them of how God rescued Israel from Egypt and fed them in the desert.
text_es_aquifer: La multitud exigió una señal milagrosa para demostrar el estatus de Jesús como Mesías. Los judíos creían que cuando apareciera el Mesías, duplicaría el gran milagro de Moisés. El maná volvería a caer, y todos lo considerarían un segundo éxodo.

text_src:
Jesus corrected the people's argument: God, not Moses, fed Israel in the wilderness. 

The most important goal in life is to seek the true bread from God. This bread is not ordinary food. It is the gift that gives eternal life. To “eat” this bread means to believe in Jesus and depend on him.

Those who receive this bread share in the life that comes from God and lasts forever.
text_es_aquifer: "Jesús corrigió el argumento de la gente": Dios, no Moisés, alimentó a Israel en el desierto. La búsqueda más importante es encontrar y consumir el verdadero pan de Dios⸢,⸣ que da vida eterna.

text_src: ⸢Sir, … give us this bread⸣: This is similar to the request of the Samaritan woman (4:15). Spiritual awakening begins with a request for God’s gift.
text_es_aquifer: "Señor, . . . danos ese pan": Esta petición es similar a la petición de la mujer samaritana (4:15). El despertar espiritual comienza con una solicitud del don de Dios.

lemma_src: I am the bread of life
text_src: In the Gospel of John, the “I am” statements reveal who Jesus is and what he came to do (see also 4:26; 8:12; 9:5; 10:7–9, 11–14; 11:25; 14:6; 15:1–5). Jesus used the words ⸢I am⸣ on purpose. These words would remind his listeners of the name of God in the Old Testament (Exodus 3:14). ⸢I am the bread of life⸣: Jesus is the true manna that came from God (John 6:38). He satisfies the spiritual hunger of those who believe in him (compare 4:10–13).
text_es_aquifer: Las declaraciones de Jesús "Yo soy" en Juan describen la identidad y el ministerio de Jesús (ver también 4:26, 8:12, 9:5, 10:7–9, 11–14; 11:25, 14:6, 15:1–5). Jesús usó intencionalmente una frase que haría que sus oyentes pensaran en el nombre del Antiguo Testamento para Dios (Éxodo 3:14). • "Yo soy el pan de vida": Jesús es el verdadero maná que descendió de Dios (Juan 6:38). Él satisface el hambre espiritual de aquellos que creen en él (cf. 4:10–13).

text_src: ⸢Everyone the Father gives Me⸣: God acts to bring people to Jesus so that they believe in him.
text_es_aquifer: "aquellos que el Padre ha dado": Dios mueve los corazones de las personas, llevándolas a Jesús.

text_src: The mission of Jesus is sure to succeed. God sent Jesus and calls people to follow him (6:37, 38, 44). Those who come to him are secure in the promise Jesus gave that he will not reject them or lose them (6:39).
text_es_aquifer: La misión de Jesús en el mundo seguramente tendrá éxito. Dios envió a Jesús (6:38) y llama a las personas a seguirlo (6:37, 44). Aquellos que vienen a él están seguros en la promesa de Jesús de que no los rechazará ni los perderá (6:39).

text_src:
When Jesus called himself ⸢the bread that came down from heaven⸣, the crowd had to make a decision. ⸢Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph⸣: The people questioned Jesus because they thought they knew him and his family.

Their familiarity with him made his claims seem strange and unbelievable. Since they saw him as an ordinary man from their town, they struggled to accept what he said about himself.
text_es_aquifer: Cuando Jesús se identificó como el verdadero pan . . . del cielo⸢,⸣ la multitud enfrentó una decisión. • "¿No es este . . . el hijo de José?" Tropezaron porque su familiaridad con Jesús hizo que sus afirmaciones parecieran extravagantes.

text_src: ⸢Stop grumbling⸣: Instead of defending himself against their complaint, Jesus addresses their lack of spiritual receptivity (their openness to God; see 6:42). Those who love the Father and listen to him will believe in Jesus.
text_es_aquifer: "Deja de quejarte": En lugar de defenderse contra su queja (6:42), Jesús se dirige al problema de su receptividad espiritual. Aquellos que aman al Padre y lo escuchan creerán en Jesús.

text_src:
Jesus connected the manna of the exodus story with himself. Then he said why he was different from the manna the Israelites received from God. 

The Israelites remained mortal and they all died⸢.⸣ But the bread from heaven (Jesus himself) provides eternal life (6:47, 51, 58).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús conectó el maná del Éxodo consigo mismo, luego señaló una diferencia importante: Los israelitas siguieron siendo mortales y todos murieron⸢,⸣ mientras que el pan del cielo (Jesús mismo) proporciona vida eterna (6:47, 51, 58).

text_src: ⸢this bread … is My flesh⸣: The gift that gives life is now made clear. On the cross, Jesus gave his body so that the world might receive life.
text_es_aquifer: "Este pan . . . es mi carne": El regalo que trae vida ahora está revelado. En la cruz, Jesús ofreció su carne por la vida del mundo.

text_src:
⸢eats My flesh and drinks My blood⸣: Jesus answered the question the people asked (6:52). His words pointed ahead to the Lord’s Supper, which would come later (see Luke 22:19). In Jewish speech, the phrase “flesh and blood” referred to the whole person. In this context, Jesus was calling people to receive him fully by completely believing in him.

Ever since the Protestant Reformation, there have been three main interpretations of the words of Jesus about the bread and wine: Transubstantiation: The bread and wine are believed to change into the actual body and blood of Christ, while still appearing to be bread and wine.Real Presence: Christ is understood to be truly present in the sacrament in a mysterious but real way that is beyond human understanding.Memorial or Symbolic View: The bread and wine are seen as symbols. The act of sharing them recalls Christ’s death and resurrection, and believers receive spiritual benefit through faith.
text_es_aquifer:
"Come mi carne . . . bebe mi sangre": Jesús respondió la pregunta que la gente hizo (6:52). Sus palabras insinuaban la Cena del Señor que estaba por venir (ver Lucas 22:19). Dado que “carne y sangre” era un modismo judío para referirse a la persona completa, Jesús podría haber estado llamando a la gente a consumirlo completamente creyendo plenamente en él. 

Desde la Reforma, han habido tres interpretaciones dominantes de las declaraciones de Jesús sobre el pan y el vino: (1) que el pan y el vino se transforman en el cuerpo y la sangre reales de Jesucristo (transubstanciación); (2) que Cristo está verdaderamente presente en el sacramento de una manera misteriosa pero real que está más allá de la comprensión humana (presencia real); (3) que el pan y el vino simbolizan el cuerpo y la sangre de Cristo, beneficiando al receptor a través del Espíritu por la fe (simbolismo).

text_src: What Jesus said was shocking and offensive (6:53–58; see Genesis 9:4–5). It was hard for his disciples and the crowd to understand. Should they take him literally? How could they eat his flesh? Jesus answers in John 6:63.
text_es_aquifer: El lenguaje de Jesús (6:53–58) fue impactante, ofensivo (ver Gn 9:4–5) y difícil de entender para sus discípulos, al igual que para la multitud. ¿Debían tomarlo literalmente? ¿Cómo comerían su carne? La respuesta de Jesús está en Juan 6:63.

text_src: The true source of the gift Jesus gives is the Holy Spirit, not human effort. In this context,⸢ the flesh⸣ refers to what humans can do on their own. Life and understanding come through the gift of the Spirit (see 14:15–20; 20:21–22). True life is found only when the Holy Spirit gives life to people.
text_es_aquifer: La esencia del regalo de Jesús se encuentra solo en el Espíritu Santo⸢,⸣ no en el esfuerzo humano (literalmente "la carne"). La vida y la comprensión vienen a través del don del Espíritu (ver 14:15–20, 20:21–22). La verdadera vida solo se puede encontrar cuando el Espíritu Santo infunde la vida humana.

text_src: ⸢no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him⸣ (see 6:44): Only God’s light can shine into the deep darkness of the world.
text_es_aquifer: "Ninguno puede venir a mí, si el Padre que me envió no le trajere" (ver 6:44): Solo la luz de Dios puede penetrar la profunda oscuridad del mundo.

text_src: Simon Peter often spoke on behalf of the 12 apostles (see also Matthew 14:28–29; 16:16; 17:4; 18:21; 19:27; 26:33–35).
text_es_aquifer: Simón Pedro a menudo servía como portavoz de los Doce (ver también Mateo 14:28–29, 16:16, 17:4, 18:21, 19:27, 26:33–35).

text_src:
Once again, Jesus showed supernatural knowledge (knowledge beyond normal human ability; see 1:47–49; 4:16–19). He knew what was in people’s hearts (their innermost selves) and what would happen in the future.

Jesus knew that Judas would betray him. Judas later betrayed Jesus to the authorities (12:4; 13:2; Matthew 26:14–16). ⸢Iscariot⸣ means “man from Kerioth.” Kerioth was the home village of Judas’s family.
text_es_aquifer: Una vez más, Jesús demostró conocimiento sobrenatural (ver 1:47–49, 4:16–19). Judas trabajaría para el mal y traicionaría a Jesús ante las autoridades (12:4, 13:2, Mt 26:14–16). • Iscariote significa "hombre de Kerioth", el pueblo natal de la familia de Judas.

text_src: This chapter describes Jesus at the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus used parts of the feast to reveal his true identity to his fellow Jews and to show that he had fulfilled the feast's essential meaning (see 7:37–39; 8:12).
text_es_aquifer: Este capítulo es otro relato de Jesús durante una festividad judía, la Fiesta de los Tabernáculos. Jesús utilizó elementos de la festividad para revelar su verdadera identidad a sus compatriotas judíos y mostrar que había cumplido con el significado esencial de la festividad (ver 7:37–39, 8:12).

text_src:
The law of Moses required Jewish men to come to the temple for the Feast of Tabernacles (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16). This annual seven-day autumn harvest feast happened in Jerusalem six months after Passover (John 6:4). 

During the feast, people lived in temporary shelters to remember the tents Israel used during their 40 years in the wilderness.
text_es_aquifer: Los hombres judíos debían venir al Templo para el Festival de los Tabernáculos (Éxodo 23:14–17, Deuteronomio 16:16), un festival anual de la cosecha de otoño de siete días en Jerusalén, seis meses después de la Pascua (Juan 6:4). La gente vivía en refugios temporales durante los siete días como recordatorio de las tiendas que Israel usó durante cuarenta años en el desierto.

text_src: The brothers of Jesus reminded him of his religious duty to go to the festival (see also Mark 3:31). Their words carried a cynical tone because at this time they did not believe in him (John 7:5).
text_es_aquifer: Los hermanos de Jesús (ver también Marcos 3:31) le recordaron su obligación religiosa de celebrar el festival. Sus palabras eran cínicas porque en ese momento no creían en él (Juan 7:5).

text_src:
⸢My time has not yet come⸣: Jesus said that it was not the right time for him to go publicly to Jerusalem.

Later, however, he did go to the city. He went quietly and not in a public way (7:10; compare study note on 12:23).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús dijo que no era el momento adecuado para que él fuera públicamente a Jerusalén, aunque más tarde fue en secreto (7:10, cf. nota de estudio sobre 12:23).

text_src:
They wondered how he could teach with such understanding.

Jesus had not studied under a well-known rabbi (a Jewish teacher of the law). Instead, he said that his teaching came from his heavenly Father.

This was different from many Jewish teachers. For example, Peter and John were known as untrained men (Acts 4:13). In contrast, Paul had studied under a respected teacher (Acts 22:3).
text_es_aquifer: Los líderes querían que Jesús mostrara su identidad. Jesús no había sido entrenado bajo un rabino, sino que fue enseñado por su Padre celestial (cf. Pedro y Juan, Hechos 4:13, contraste con Pablo, Hechos 22:3).

text_src:
People who truly want to follow God's will accept Jesus and his teachings (see also 5:42–47). 

In contrast, those who focus only on the values and desires of this world are not open to Christ. When people care more about human approval, power, or temporary success, they struggle to receive his message.
text_es_aquifer: Aquellos que realmente quieren hacer la voluntad de Dios reciben y aceptan a Jesús y su enseñanza (ver también 5:42–47). Aquellos que se enfocan en el mundo, por el contrario, no son receptivos a Cristo.

text_src:
⸢Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it⸣: The Jewish leaders were proud of the law of Moses. They believed they carefully obeyed it.

However, Jesus pointed out a serious problem. While they honored the law in words, they were planning to kill him. In doing so, they were breaking the law (Exodus 20:13).
text_es_aquifer: "Moisés les dio la ley, ¡pero ninguno de ustedes la obedece!" Los líderes judíos estaban orgullosos de la ley de Moisés, pero irónicamente, al intentar matar a Jesús, estaban quebrantando la ley (Éxodo 20:13).

text_src: ⸢You have a demon⸣: See 8:48–52; 10:20–21.
text_es_aquifer: "¡Estás poseído por un demonio!" Ver 8:48–52, 10:20–21.

text_src:
The law required circumcision on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). It allowed a boy to be circumcised even if that day was the Sabbath. 

Jesus argued in the way many rabbis did. They reasoned from the lesser to the greater. If a smaller religious act, such as circumcision, was allowed on the Sabbath, then a greater act, such as making a whole person well, should also be allowed.
text_es_aquifer: La ley requería la circuncisión en el octavo día (Lv 12:3) y permitía que un niño fuera circuncidado incluso si ese día caía en el sábado. Jesús argumentó como lo haría un rabino, de “lo menor a lo mayor,” usando la circuncisión como un precedente para la curación, ambas son obras religiosas.

text_src:
Some people in the crowd believed they knew where Jesus came from. Because they could trace his earthly origins, they thought he could not be the Messiah.

They expected the Messiah to appear suddenly and in a mysterious way. Since Jesus had grown up among them, they assumed he did not fit their expectations.
text_es_aquifer: Algunos de la multitud pensaron que, dado que podían rastrear los orígenes terrenales de Jesús, él no podía ser el Mesías. Creían que el Mesías simplemente aparecería.

text_src:
⸢I am from Him⸣: Instead of answering questions about where he grew up (7:27, 40–44), Jesus spoke about where he truly came from. He pointed to his heavenly origin.

He said that he was sent by God. This was a bold claim.

The religious leaders understood what he meant. Because of this, they tried to arrest him. They believed he was speaking in a way that dishonored God (7:30; compare 10:30–33).
text_es_aquifer: "Yo vengo de él": Jesús evitó la especulación (7:27, 40–44) sobre sus orígenes terrenales y se centró en sus orígenes celestiales. Su asombrosa afirmación provocó que los líderes religiosos intentaran arrestarlo por blasfemia (7:30, cp. 10:30–33).

lemma_src: His hour had not yet come
text_src:
⸢His hour had not yet come⸣: Those who opposed Jesus could not arrest him. This was because, according to God's plan, the time for Jesus to be glorified on the cross had not yet come (see study note on 12:23; see also 10:17–18; 18:6–8). 

All four arrest scenes in 7:1–8:59 emphasize that Jesus was in control, not the Jewish leaders.
text_es_aquifer: Los oponentes de Jesús no lograron arrestarlo porque en el plan soberano de Dios, su momento⸢,⸣ cuando sería glorificado en la cruz, aún no había llegado (ver nota de estudio en 12:23, ver también 10:17–18, 18:6–8). Las cuatro escenas de arresto en 7:1–8:59 enfatizan que Jesús tenía el control, no los líderes judíos.

text_src: Jesus announced his return to the one who sent him, the Father in heaven (17:1–7). But the Pharisees misunderstood him. They thought he was leaving Judea to visit the Gentiles (non-Jewish people). These were people whom Pharisees would never visit. After Jesus returned to the Father, the Jewish leaders would no longer be able to find him.⸢and where I am, you cannot come⸣: These Pharisees, still in spiritual darkness, could not enter heaven. So Jesus would be beyond their reach there.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús anunció su regreso a quien lo envió, el Padre en el cielo (17:1–7). Sin embargo, los fariseos malinterpretaron, pensando que se iba de Judea para ir entre los gentiles (a quienes los fariseos nunca visitarían). • Los líderes no encontrarían a Jesús después de su ascensión. • "no pueden ir a donde yo voy": Estos fariseos, aún en la oscuridad, no podían entrar al cielo, por lo que Jesús estaría fuera de su alcance allí.

text_src:
⸢Living water⸣: See 4:10–14. A water ceremony was held each day during the Feast of Tabernacles, with prayer for God to send rain in the late autumn. 

The final day, called ⸢the great day⸣, was the feast's most important moment. On this day, they repeated the ceremony seven times. They poured water over the altar while Levites sang Isaiah 12:3 (see Zechariah 14:8; see also ⸢Mishnah Sukkah⸣ chapter 4). ⸢If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink⸣: Jesus fulfilled an important part of the Feast of Tabernacles. He himself is the source of living water, available to anyone who believes.
text_es_aquifer: "Agua viva": Ver 4:10–14. Se realizaba una ceremonia del agua cada día durante el Festival de los Tabernáculos, con oración para que Dios enviara lluvia a finales del otoño. El último día, llamado “el gran día,” era el clímax del festival⸢,⸣ cuando la ceremonia se repetía siete veces. Se vertía agua sobre el altar mientras los levitas cantaban Is 12:3 (ver Zc 14:8, ver también ⸢Mishnah Sukkah,⸣ cap. 4). • "¡Cualquiera que tenga sed puede venir a mí!" Jesús cumplió un elemento esencial en el Festival de los Tabernáculos. Él mismo es la fuente de agua viva, disponible para cualquiera que crea

text_src:
In the death and resurrection of Jesus, his life was given for others, and the Holy Spirit was given to believers.

When Jesus was crucified, blood and water flowed from his side (see 19:34). This event points to the gift of life that comes through his death.

After he rose from the dead, he breathed on his disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit (20:22). In this way, his life and the Spirit were poured out for his followers.
text_es_aquifer: En la crucifixión y resurrección de Jesús, su vida y el Espíritu fueron derramados (ver 19:34, 20:22).

text_src: These Jews were not like the crowd who thought the Christ (the Messiah) would have a mysterious appearance (7:25–27). They believed the prophecy that God's chosen ruler would come from Bethlehem in Judea (see Micah 5:2). However, they struggled with the fact that Jesus seemed to be from Galilee, where he grew up.
text_es_aquifer: Estos judíos, diferentes de la multitud (7:25–27) que pensaban que el Mesías aparecería misteriosamente, creían en la profecía de que el Mesías sería de Belén de Judea (ver Mi 5:2). Sin embargo, tropezaron con el hecho de que Jesús parecía ser de Galilea⸢,⸣ donde creció.

text_src: The story ends with Jewish leaders feeling frustrated and the people being divided over their opinion of Jesus (compare 7:25–27, 31–32). ⸢officers returned⸣: See 7:32.
text_es_aquifer: La historia concluye con los líderes judíos frustrados y el mundo dividido sobre Jesús (cp. 7:25–27, 31–32). • "alguaciles regresaron": Ver 7:32.

text_src:
Nicodemus was likely starting to believe in Jesus (see 3:1–21; 19:38–42). Some leaders claimed that none of the Pharisees believed in Jesus (7:48). They spoke as if only the crowd, whom the leaders believed did not understand the law, supported him.

However, Nicodemus shows that this was not completely true. Not only the people in the crowd, but also some Pharisees were beginning to believe in him.
text_es_aquifer: Nicodemo probablemente estaba en el proceso de llegar a la fe (ver 3:1–21, 19:38–42). Contrario a la implicación de 7:48, algunos de los fariseos, no solo la multitud ignorante, creyeron en Jesús.

text_src: ⸢no prophet comes out of Galilee⸣: The Jewish leaders were apparently unaware that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, not in Galilee (see Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:1–7).
text_es_aquifer: "¡Ningún profeta viene de Galilea!" Los líderes judíos aparentemente no sabían que Jesús había nacido en Belén de Judea, no en Galilea (ver Mateo 2:1, Lucas 2:1–7).

text_src: It is likely that someone added this story to John's Gospel later, since it is not in the earliest Greek manuscripts. However, it is likely a true story from the life of Jesus.
text_es_aquifer: Esta historia, una adición posterior al Evangelio de Juan, no aparece en los primeros manuscritos griegos. Sin embargo, es probable que sea una historia auténtica de la vida de Jesús.

text_src: ⸢The scribes and Pharisees⸣: The teachers of religious law were Jewish scholars. They specialized in the Old Testament law and oral traditions that explained it.
text_es_aquifer: Los maestros de la ley religiosa eran eruditos judíos que se especializaban en conocer la ley del Antiguo Testamento y las tradiciones orales que interpretaban la ley.

text_src: The form of the Greek sentence emphasizes the legal claim against the woman. She had been caught while committing the sin of adultery. The law required two witnesses and carefully outlined what evidence was needed.
text_es_aquifer: La forma de la frase griega enfatiza la acusación legal contra la mujer. Había sido sorprendida cometiendo el pecado de adulterio. La ley requería dos testigos y detallaba cuidadosamente qué evidencia era necesaria.

text_src:
⸢In the Law Moses commanded us to stone⸣: This suggests the woman was engaged or married (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:23–24). The law also indicates that the man who sinned with her must die as well. But these Jewish religious leaders ignored that part of the law. They could have dealt with the situation privately to avoid shaming her. But their real intention was to condemn Jesus instead. They asked him, ⸢So what do you say?⸣ 

Would he neglect the law since he had a reputation for mercy? Or would he ignore the woman’s tragedy?
text_es_aquifer: El requisito de la ley … apedrearla indica que la mujer estaba comprometida o casada (Lv 20:10; Dt 22:23–24). La ley también establecía que su amante debía ser asesinado con ella, pero estos líderes religiosos aparentemente ignoraron su obligación con esa parte del estatuto. • Estos hombres podrían haber tratado con la mujer en privado y evitarle la vergüenza pública, pero Jesús era su verdadero objetivo mientras exigían, "Tú, pues, ¿qué dices?". ¿Ignoraría la ley dado que tenía una reputación de misericordia? ¿O ignoraría la tragedia de la mujer?

text_src: We cannot know what Jesus wrote in the dust. Some scholars suggest he wrote down the sins of those who were accusing the woman.
text_es_aquifer: Es imposible saber qué escribió Jesús en el polvo. Se ha sugerido que escribió los pecados de los acusadores.

text_src: The answer Jesus gave did not mean that someone who makes an accusation must be morally perfect to make legal claims. He referred to ⸢him⸣ ⸢who is without sin⸣ to point to the motives of those accusing her.
text_es_aquifer: La respuesta de Jesús no significaba que un acusador tuviera que ser moralmente perfecto para hacer acusaciones legales. Su referencia a quien nunca ha pecado señala los motivos de los acusadores.

text_src: ⸢they began to go away one by one⸣: One of the people accusing her left, then another, followed by several people who had been standing there watching what was happening.
text_es_aquifer: El jurado se desmoronó mientras se escabullían. Un acusador se fue, seguido por otro, y luego una sucesión de transeúntes.

text_src: ⸢neither do I⸣: Jesus spoke words of assurance, but this did not suggest that the woman was innocent. Jesus takes sin and judgment seriously, but he shows grace and forgiveness to those overcome by sin.
text_es_aquifer: "Yo tampoco": Las palabras de seguridad de Jesús no sugerían que la mujer fuera inocente. Jesús ve el pecado y el juicio con seriedad, pero mira con gracia y perdón a aquellos atrapados en las garras del pecado.

text_src: During the Festival of Tabernacles, people filled 16 gold bowls in the temple's inner courts with oil and lit them. Jesus stood under these lights in the temple and said that he was now the source of the light of the world (8:20). The light of Jesus brings salvation to both Israel and the world, regardless of race or location.
text_es_aquifer: Durante el Festival de los Refugios, dieciséis cuencos de oro en los patios interiores del Templo se llenaron de aceite y se encendieron. Jesús se paró debajo de estas luces en el Templo (8:20) y dijo que ahora él era la fuente de la luz. La luz de Jesús trae salvación no solo a Israel sino al mundo⸢,⸣ sin importar raza o lugar.

text_src: The debate about whether Jesus is the Messiah continues from 7:52. Jesus remained at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem. During the feast, the conflicts Jesus encountered in chapter 7 continued and intensified.
text_es_aquifer: El debate sobre si Jesús es el Mesías continúa desde 7:52. Jesús todavía estaba en el Festival de los Tabernáculos en Jerusalén. Durante el festival, los conflictos que Jesús había soportado en el capítulo 7 continuaron e intensificaron.

text_src: The Pharisees argued that what Jesus was saying about himself was not valid because Jewish law requires more than one witness (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare John 5:31–32; see 8:17).
text_es_aquifer: Los fariseos afirmaron que las declaraciones de Jesús no eran válidas porque la ley judía (Dt 19:15) requiere más de un testigo (cf. Juan 5:31–32, ver 8:17).

text_src: Jesus responded to the Pharisees' accusations. He said he could make these claims about himself because he knew both his origin and his destination were heaven. He then said the most important witness for his case was his Father who sent him (8:16).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús respondió a las acusaciones de los fariseos, diciendo que podía hacer tales afirmaciones sobre sí mismo porque conocía tanto su origen (cielo) como su destino (cielo). Luego señaló al testigo más vital para su caso, su Padre que lo envió (8:16).

text_src: Throughout the feast, those listening to Jesus proved they were in darkness as they misunderstood him. They wanted to meet the father of Jesus, who is God. Since they did not truly know God, they were unable to understand Jesus.
text_es_aquifer: Durante el festival, la audiencia de Jesús demostró que estaban en la oscuridad ya que lo malinterpretaron. Querían conocer al padre de Jesús⸢,⸣ que es Dios. Como no conocían verdaderamente a Dios, no podían entender a Jesús.

text_src: The treasury was in the section of the temple called the Court of the Women. Jesus often taught there so both men and women could listen (Mark 12:41). ⸢His hour⸣: See notes on John 2:4; 12:23.
text_es_aquifer: El Tesoro estaba ubicado en la sección del Templo llamada el Patio de las Mujeres. Jesús a menudo enseñaba allí para que tanto hombres como mujeres pudieran escucharlo (Marcos 12:41). • "su tiempo": Ver notas sobre Juan 2:4, 12:23.

text_src: In the earlier debate at the feast, people questioned where Jesus came from (7:27). Here, Jesus talked about returning to where he came from (heaven). However, once again, his words were misunderstood by the people listening.
text_es_aquifer: En el debate anterior en el festival, los orígenes de Jesús estaban en cuestión (7:27). Aquí, Jesús mencionó irse al lugar de donde vino, es decir, el cielo. Sin embargo, una vez más, sus palabras fueron malinterpretadas.

text_src:
Jesus told his listeners that they were ⸢from below,⸣ while he was ⸢from above ⸣(3:31; see study note on 3:3).

⸢From below⸣ refers to human life limited to this world. ⸢From above⸣ refers to heaven and to God’s realm.

Because they were thinking only in earthly terms, they could not understand what Jesus meant. His origin and authority came from God.
text_es_aquifer: Los oyentes de Jesús eran de abajo⸢;⸣ no podían comprender el significado de Jesús porque él era de arriba (3:31, ver nota de estudio sobre 3:3).

text_src: ⸢unless you believe that I am He⸣: Jesus used God's divine name (see 4:26; Exodus 3:14). His listeners did not fully understand the meaning of his words (John 8:25). ⸢die in your sins⸣: Jesus is the light who has come into the world. His presence offers the only way of salvation. If people reject him, they remain in darkness and do not receive life.
text_es_aquifer: "a menos que creas que Yo soy quien afirmo ser": Jesús usó el nombre divino de Dios (ver 4:26, Éxodo 3:14), pero los oyentes no captaron el matiz (Juan 8:25). • "morir en tus pecados": La presencia de Jesús en el mundo, como la luz que penetra la oscuridad, es la única oportunidad de salvación para el mundo.

text_src: ⸢Who are you?⸣: Later, they understood what he was claiming about himself. They believed he was showing dishonor toward God. Because of this, they tried to stone him (8:59).
text_es_aquifer: "¿Quién eres tú?" Luego entendieron y trataron de apedrear a Jesús por blasfemia (8:59).

text_src:
The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus as predicting his death three times (for example, Mark 8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). 

The Gospel of John presents this theme in a different way. Jesus speaks about being ⸢lifted up⸣ (John 3:14; 8:28; 12:33–34). This phrase refers to his crucifixion and also to his glory. The Father directs the course of events. The death of Jesus did not happen by accident, but according to God’s plan.
text_es_aquifer: Los Evangelios sinópticos describen a Jesús prediciendo su muerte tres veces (por ejemplo, Marcos 8:31, 9:31, 10:33–34). Juan hace un paralelo (Juan 3:14, 8:28, 12:33–34), mostrando que el Padre gobierna el destino de su Hijo.

text_src:
Once again, the crowd at the feast was divided. Earlier, the discussion had ended with plans to arrest Jesus (8:20). Now many people believed in him. They were persuaded that he was speaking the truth.

However, when Jesus spoke more clearly about who he really was, their faith was tested. As his full identity became known, some struggled to accept his words (8:31–59).
text_es_aquifer: Una vez más, el público del festival estaba dividido. Anteriormente, el debate concluyó con planes para arrestar a Jesús (8:20). Ahora muchos . . . creyeron en él, convencidos de que estaba diciendo la verdad. Sin embargo, una vez que se reveló completamente la identidad de Jesús, su fe fue dolorosamente desafiada (8:31–59).

text_src: Discipleship involves more than just knowing who Jesus is. It also requires obeying his teachings (3:36; 14:15, 21, 23; 15:10). Because Jesus is the truth, knowing him helps a person understand what is true and what is false (14:6).⸢set you free⸣: The truth frees a person from darkness, lies, and sin.
text_es_aquifer: El discipulado es más que saber quién es Jesús. También se trata de obedecer sus enseñanzas (3:36, 14:15, 21, 23; 15:10). • Porque Jesús es la verdad (14:6), conocerlo trae discernimiento de lo que es verdadero y lo que es falso. • "te hará libre": La verdad trae libertad de la oscuridad, la falsedad y el pecado.

text_src:
Jesus challenged a common belief about Israel as God’s chosen people. Many thought that being descendants of Abraham gave them special privilege and protection.

Instead of seeing this heritage as a responsibility to obey God, some treated it as a guarantee of safety. However, the prophets had warned that privilege brings accountability (compare Amos 3:1–15). The people did not understand what Jesus meant by ⸢set free⸣. He was not talking about freedom from human slavery. He meant freedom from spiritual slavery to sin (John 8:34). 

True freedom comes through the truth. It does not come from family history or religious background (8:32; Romans 6:17; 8:2; 1 John 3:4, 8, 9).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús desafió una suposición ampliamente aceptada sobre el estatus de Israel como el pueblo elegido de Dios. Su herencia como descendientes de Abraham había inspirado sentimientos de privilegio e inmunidad en lugar de obligación y responsabilidad (cp. Amós 3:1–15). • La gente malinterpretó lo que significaba ser liberado. Jesús no se refería a la libertad de la esclavitud humana; él se refería a la liberación de la esclavitud espiritual al pecado (Juan 8:34). La verdad y no su herencia religiosa, los liberaría (8:32, Rm 6:17, 8:2, 1 Jn 3:4, 8, 9).

text_src: Jesus explained his argument: If Israel is a spiritual slave, it has the same insecurity as any slave in a household. Family members are secure, but slaves are not. Only Jesus can change the status of those in spiritual slavery, making them free and secure.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús explicó la lógica de su argumento: Si Israel es un esclavo espiritual⸢,⸣ tiene la misma inseguridad que cualquier esclavo en un hogar. Los miembros de una familia son seguros, los esclavos no. Solo Jesús puede cambiar el status de aquellos en esclavitud espiritual y hacerlos libres y seguros.

text_src:
The leaders' plan to kill Jesus revealed their true identity (5:18). They were part of a different spiritual family, and their spiritual father was not Jesus's Father. They were relying on the fact that their ancestral father was Abraham, but Jesus challenged their spiritual heritage. 

The most important part of his challenge comes in 8:44.
text_es_aquifer: El complot de los líderes para matar a Jesús (5:18) desenmascaró su verdadera identidad. Pertenecían a una casa diferente, y su padre no era el Padre de Jesús. Confiaban en el hecho de que su padre ancestral era Abraham, pero Jesús desafió su linaje espiritual. El clímax de su desafío llega en 8:44.

text_src: ⸢your father⸣: Jesus knew who controlled them. ⸢We are not illegitimate children⸣: This statement acted as both a defense and an attack. The Greek text emphasizes the pronoun ⸢we⸣. In other words, “⸢We⸣ [in contrast to ⸢you⸣] ⸢are not illegitimate.⸣” They are suggesting that Jesus was illegitimate (see Matthew 1:18–25).
text_es_aquifer: "tu verdadero padre": Jesús sabía quién los controlaba. • "¡Nosotros no somos hijos ilegítimos!" Esto era tanto una defensa como un ataque. En griego, el pronombre "nosotros" es enfático: “Nosotros [en contraste con ustedes] no somos ilegítimos,” implicando que Jesús era ilegítimo (ver Mateo 1:18–25).

text_src: Since the unbelieving people did not love Jesus (8:42; 1 John 5:1), they were not children of the Father in heaven who sent his beloved Son (John 8:47). Their desire to kill God’s Son showed their true spiritual heritage. This was the work of the devil, who brought death to the world (see Genesis 3:1–20; Romans 5:12–14).
text_es_aquifer: Como la gente incrédula no amaba a Jesús (8:42, 1 Jn 5:1), no eran hijos del Padre en el cielo que envió a su amado Hijo (Juan 8:47). Su verdadera ascendencia espiritual se reveló en su deseo de matar al Hijo de Dios. Esta era la obra del diablo⸢,⸣ quien trajo la muerte al mundo (ver Gn 3:1–20, Rm 5:12–14).

text_src:
By calling Jesus a Samaritan with a demon, his opponents used a racial insult to dismiss his accusations (see study note on 4:4–6). They claimed Jesus was demon-possessed to counter his claim that they belonged to Satan (also 7:20; 8:52; 10:20; 8:44). 

Jesus rightly replied that these words were deeply offensive. In fact, it was a serious and unforgivable offense (Mark 3:22–29).
text_es_aquifer: Al llamar a Jesús un diablo samaritano⸢,⸣ sus oponentes devolvieron sus acusaciones con un insulto racial (ver nota de estudio en 4:4–6). Su declaración de que Jesús estaba poseído por un demonio (también 7:20, 8:52, 10:20) contradecía su afirmación de que ellos estaban vinculados a Satanás (8:44). Jesús respondió correctamente que estas palabras eran un profundo deshonor. De hecho, fue una ofensa grave e imperdonable (Marcos 3:22–29).

text_src: ⸢Who do You claim to be?⸣: This question was hostile and aggressive. However, if Jesus is immortal, ruling over life and death, then he is greater than Abraham⸢,⸣ the prophets⸢,⸣ or any of the greatest people in Israel’s history (8:58).
text_es_aquifer: "¿Quién te crees que eres?" Esta pregunta era antagónica y agresiva. Sin embargo, si Jesús es inmortal, gobernando sobre la vida y la muerte, entonces es mayor que Abraham⸢,⸣ los profetas⸢,⸣ o cualquiera de las personas más grandes en la historia de Israel (8:58).

text_src: Like his opponents, Jesus appealed to Abraham. Rabbis taught that God had given Abraham prophetic insight, teaching him about the coming age of the Messiah.
text_es_aquifer: Al igual que sus oponentes, Jesús apeló a Abraham. Los rabinos enseñaban que Dios le había dado a Abraham una visión profética, enseñándole sobre la era venidera del Mesías.

text_src: ⸢You are not yet fifty years old⸣: The Jewish leaders misunderstood Jesus. Jesus was not talking about his physical age. He was speaking about his divine pre-existence (his existence before he was born as a human).
text_es_aquifer: "Aún no tienes ni cincuenta años": Los líderes judíos malinterpretaron a Jesús: Él estaba hablando de su preexistencia divina, no de su edad física.

text_src: ⸢before Abraham was born, I am!⸣:⸢ ⸣The life of Jesus spans the past from before creation and continues forever (1:1–2). ⸢I am⸣: This title recalls the name of God revealed to Moses at Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:14; compare John 4:26; Isaiah 43:11–13; 48:12).
text_es_aquifer: "antes de que Abraham naciera, ¡Yo Soy!" La vida de Jesús abarca el pasado desde antes de la creación (1:1–2) y se extiende más allá del presente hacia la eternidad. • "Yo Soy": Este título recuerda el nombre de Dios dado en el Monte Sinaí (Éxodo 3:14, cp. Juan 4:26, Isaías 43:11–13, 48:12).

text_src: Those listening to Jesus finally understood his claim to be God (8:58). Because of this, they became very angry. They believed they had heard blasphemy (words that dishonored God) and picked up stones to throw at him⸢,⸣ which was the proper legal response (Leviticus 24:16). Jesus was hidden from them because God had chosen a different time for his death (see study note on John 12:23; see also 7:30, 44; Luke 4:29–30).
text_es_aquifer: La audiencia de Jesús finalmente entendió su afirmación de divinidad (8:58), y se enfurecieron. Creyeron haber escuchado blasfemia y recogieron piedras para arrojárselas⸢,⸣ lo cual era la respuesta legal adecuada (Lv 24:16). • Jesús fue ocultado de ellos porque Dios había designado un momento diferente para su muerte (ver nota de estudio sobre Juan 12:23, ver también 7:30, 44; Lucas 4:29–30).

text_src:
At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus claimed to be the light of the world (chapters 7–8; see 8:12). Now John tells about Jesus giving light, both physically and spiritually, to a blind man who lived in darkness (see 9:5). 

The story ends with a surprising reversal (a complete change) of roles: The man who had been blind was assumed to live in spiritual darkness. Yet he came to see and accept God’s light. The Pharisees could see with their physical eyes. People thought they were spiritually enlightened (well taught and wise). However, they refused to believe. In the end, they were shown to be spiritually blind.
text_es_aquifer: En el Festival de los Tabernáculos (cap. 7–8), Jesús afirmó ser la luz del mundo (8:12). Ahora Juan cuenta cómo Jesús dio luz, tanto física como espiritualmente, a un hombre ciego que vivía en la oscuridad (ver 9:5). La historia termina con una espléndida inversión de roles: El hombre ciego que se asumía estaba en oscuridad espiritual pudo ver la luz de Dios, mientras que los fariseos, que podían ver físicamente y se pensaba que estaban iluminados, se mostraron espiritualmente ciegos.

text_src: The disciples thought the man was born blind because of sin, either his own sin or his parents'. Jesus corrected this common belief (9:3).
text_es_aquifer: Los discípulos asumieron que el pecado de alguien, el del hombre o el de sus padres, había causado que naciera ciego. Jesús corrigió esta creencia común (9:3).

lemma_src: I am the light of the world
text_src: ⸢I am the light of the world⸣: See study note on 8:12.
text_es_aquifer: "Soy la luz del mundo": Ver nota de estudio en 8:12.

text_src: During the New Testament era, saliva was used for medical purposes (see Mark 7:32–35; 8:22–25).
text_es_aquifer: Durante la era del Nuevo Testamento, la saliva se usaba con fines médicos (ver Marcos 7:32–35, 8:22–25).

text_src: Siloam, a pool at the south end of Jerusalem, provided water for the Feast of Tabernacles ceremonies. ⸢which means “Sent”⸣: This phrase contained a double meaning: Jesus, who has been ⸢sent⸣ by God, told the blind man to wash in the pool called ⸢Sent⸣ (4:34; 5:23, 37; 7:28; 8:26; 12:44; 14:24).
text_es_aquifer: Siloé⸢,⸣ una piscina en el extremo sur de la ciudad de Jerusalén, era la fuente de agua para las ceremonias en el Festival de los Tabernáculos. • Siloé significa “enviado”: Esta frase contenía un doble significado: Jesús, quien ha sido enviado por Dios (4:34, 5:23, 37; 7:28, 8:26, 12:44, 14:24), le dijo al hombre ciego que se lavara en la piscina llamada “enviado.”

text_src: The blind man recognized Jesus and spoke with confidence about him. Jesus healed the man of his physical problem, and the man gained more spiritual understanding (9:17, 33). He became a disciple of Jesus (9:38; compare 5:11–15).
text_es_aquifer: El hombre ciego identificó a Jesús y testificó fuertemente sobre él. El hombre fue sanado de su enfermedad física, ganó una creciente percepción espiritual (9:17, 33), y se convirtió en discípulo de Jesús (9:38, cp. 5:11–15).

text_src: The Pharisees were experts in interpreting the Jewish law. So the community asked them to explain this miracle (see 1:24). Instead of celebrating the healing, these religious leaders questioned the man because Jesus had performed the miracle on the Sabbath (see 5:16–18).
text_es_aquifer: Los fariseos (ver 1:24) eran árbitros de la interpretación legal, por lo que la comunidad los buscaba para explicar este milagro. En lugar de celebrar la curación, estos líderes religiosos interrogaron al hombre porque Jesús había realizado el milagro en el sábado (ver 5:16–18).

text_src: The man had already identified his healer (9:11, 16). Now he made his own spiritual judgment, calling Jesus a prophet.
text_es_aquifer: El hombre ya había identificado a su sanador (9:11, 16). Ahora hizo su propio juicio espiritual, llamando a Jesús de profeta.

text_src:
The Pharisees wanted to dismiss the miracle. They did not want to accept that Jesus had truly healed the man.

They called the man’s parents and questioned them. They hoped the parents would deny that a real healing had taken place.
text_es_aquifer: Los fariseos querían desacreditar el milagro y esperaban que los padres del hombre negaran la curación.

text_src: His parents confirmed that their son had been born blind⸢,⸣ but they hesitated to judge how he could see because they were afraid of the social consequences.
text_es_aquifer: Sus padres confirmaron que su hijo había nacido ciego⸢,⸣ pero dudaron en juzgar cómo podía ver porque tenían miedo de las consecuencias sociales.

text_src: ⸢Give glory to God!⸣: Compare Joshua 7:19.
text_es_aquifer: "Dios debe recibir la gloria por esto": el griego dice "Da gloria a Dios⸢".⸣ Cf. Josué 7:19.

text_src: The Pharisees could not argue against the logic of the miracle (9:24–25, 30–33). So they abandoned reason and cursed him (see 9:34). The harsh division between Jesus and the religious leaders was clear. They considered those who followed Jesus to have rejected Moses and Judaism.
text_es_aquifer: Los fariseos no pudieron derrotar la lógica del signo milagroso (9:24–25, 30–33), así que abandonaron la razón y lo maldijeron (ver 9:34). • La dura división entre Jesús y los líderes religiosos era clara. Consideraban que aquellos que seguían a Jesús habían rechazado a Moisés y al judaísmo.

text_src:
The Jewish leaders did not know where Jesus came from. It made sense that the man was amazed. A healing like this had never happened before. 

The work of Jesus showed he was from God. Once people knew who he truly was, they should have believed and followed him. However, the Jewish leaders chose to ignore the truth.
text_es_aquifer: Los líderes judíos no sabían de dónde venía Jesús. El asombro del hombre era comprensible: una curación como esta no tenía precedentes. Las obras de Jesús confirmaron su origen como de Dios. Una vez que se conociera su verdadera identidad, la creencia y el discipulado deberían haber seguido, pero los líderes judíos eran deliberadamente ciegos.

text_src: Only God could give sight to someone born blind. By healing the man, Jesus gave the Jewish leaders an obvious sign that he was from God and was the Messiah (compare Psalm 146:8; Isaiah 35:5; 42:7).
text_es_aquifer: Solo Dios podría hacer algo como abrir los ojos de alguien nacido ciego. Al sanar al hombre, Jesús ofreció a los líderes judíos una señal incuestionable de que él era de Dios y era el Mesías (cp. Sl 146:8, Is 35:5, 42:7).

text_src: Discipline such as being thrown out of the synagogue was not uncommon. It brought social isolation that might require the man’s departure from the village. Such serious persecution was precisely what Jesus predicted for his followers (15:18–27; 16:2).
text_es_aquifer: La disciplina, como ser expulsado de la sinagoga, no era rara. Traía aislamiento social que podría requerir la partida del hombre del pueblo. Tal persecución seria fue precisamente lo que Jesús predijo para sus seguidores (15:18–27, 16:2).

text_src: ⸢Son of Man⸣: See 1:51; 3:13, 14; 5:27; 6:27, 53, 62; 8:28. The Greek expression translates a Hebrew and Aramaic phrase that means ⸢human being⸣. People were often unsure what Jesus meant when he used this title (see 12:34). In Daniel 7:13–14, a human figure receives authority and an eternal kingdom from God. Later Jewish tradition connected this figure with hopes for the Messiah. John uses the title ⸢Son of Man⸣ to point to Jesus as both an ordinary human being and the Messiah appointed by God.
text_es_aquifer: "Hijo del Hombre": Ver 1:51, 3:13, 14; 5:27, 6:27, 53, 62; 8:28. La expresión griega traduce una frase hebrea y aramea que significa “ser humano.”  La gente a menudo no estaba segura de lo que Jesús quería decir cuando usaba este título (ver 12:34). En Daniel 7:13–14, una figura humana recibe autoridad y un reino eterno de Dios. Más tarde, la tradición judía relacionó esta figura con las esperanzas del Mesías. Juan usa el título Hijo del Hombre para señalar a Jesús como un ser humano común y corriente y como el Mesías designado por Dios.

text_src: Jesus urged the man who had been blind to understand the miracle and recognize the one who healed him. The man immediately showed faith and honored Jesus in the same way he would honor God (9:38; compare 20:28).
text_es_aquifer: Jesús presionó al hombre que había sido ciego para que entendiera el milagro y la identidad de su sanador. Inmediatamente, el hombre expresó fe y dio a Jesús la reverencia debida solo a Dios (9:38, cp. 20:28).

text_src: ⸢Are we blind too?⸣: Jesus answered that those who claim to hold all religious truth will discover that they are blind⸢,⸣ while those who recognize their spiritual poverty will find true sight. In the story, the blind man and his family frequently confessed that they did not know, while the Pharisees repeatedly stated their confidence and remained guilty because of their religious pride. If they had confessed their ignorance and admitted their spiritual blindness, they would be guiltless. Instead, their conscious and willful rejection of Jesus established their guilt.
text_es_aquifer: "Estás diciendo que estamos ciegos?" Jesús respondió que aquellos que afirman tener toda la verdad religiosa descubrirán que están ciegos⸢,⸣ mientras que aquellos que reconocen su pobreza espiritual encontrarán la verdadera visión. En la historia, el hombre ciego y su familia frecuentemente confesaban que no sabían, mientras que los fariseos repetidamente declaraban su confianza y permanecían culpables debido a su orgullo religioso. Si hubieran confesado su ignorancia y admitido su ceguera espiritual, serían inocentes. En cambio, su rechazo consciente y voluntario de Jesús estableció su culpa.

text_src:
A shepherd in the wild would build a sheepfold. This was a pen with low stone walls topped by sharp branches, to keep his sheep safe at night. The pen had one gate (or opening in the wall) that was closed with branches. Any person or thing that came into the pen threatened the flock. A bad shepherd was like ⸢a thief and a robber⸣. He used the sheep for his own gain and did not care for them. Bad shepherds took the sheep’s milk and wool for themselves. They killed the sheep without guaranteeing their safety (Ezekiel 34:3; see Isaiah 56:11; Jeremiah 23:1–4). 

These words were the strongest rebuke Jesus spoke against the Jewish leaders.
text_es_aquifer: Un pastor del desierto construiría un redil⸢,⸣ un corral con paredes bajas de piedra coronadas por ramas espinosas, para guardar sus ovejas por la noche y protegerlas del peligro. • El corral tenía una puerta (o abertura en la pared) que se cerraba con ramas. Cualquier invasión del corral era una amenaza para el rebaño. • Un mal pastor era como un ladrón y un bandido. Explotaba a las ovejas para sus propios intereses y no se preocupaba por ellas ni las cuidaba. Los malos pastores tomaban la leche y la lana de las ovejas para sí mismos y sacrificaban a las ovejas sin proporcionar seguridad al animal (Ezequiel 34:3, ver Isaías 56:11, Jeremías 23:1–4). Esta fue la acusación más dura de Jesús contra los líderes judíos.

text_src:
This illustration of a shepherd and his sheep comes from a Middle Eastern perspective of shepherding and Old Testament traditions in first-century AD Jewish culture. God was the shepherd of Israel (Genesis 49:24; Psalms 23; 78:52–53; Isaiah 40:10–11). 

Spiritual and political leaders of Israel were also shepherds of God’s people, the flock of God (Isaiah 56:9–12; Jeremiah 23:1–4; Ezekiel 34). 

Jesus spoke these words during the Feast of Dedication (see John 10:22). At that time, people remembered both faithful and unfaithful leaders in Israel’s history.

In this setting, Jesus addressed the theme of shepherds. He spoke in a way that echoes Ezekiel 34, where God condemns bad shepherds and promises to care for his people himself. Jesus then identified himself as the good shepherd (John 10:11–14).
text_es_aquifer: Esta ilustración de un pastor y sus ovejas asume una comprensión del pastoreo del Medio Oriente y se basa en la tradición del Antiguo Testamento profundamente arraigada en la cultura judía del primer siglo. Dios era el pastor de Israel (Gn 49:24, Sal 23, 78:52–53, Is 40:10–11). Los líderes espirituales y políticos de Israel también eran pastores del pueblo de Dios, el rebaño de Dios (Is 56:9–12, Jr 23:1–4; Ez 34). El sermón de Jesús se basa en la ocasión de Hanukkah (ver Jn 10:22) para abordar el tema de los pastores, utilizando este festival como una oportunidad para reflexionar sobre los líderes de Israel (“pastores”) a la luz de Ez 34. Jesús se presenta a sí mismo como el buen pastor (Jn 10:11–14).

text_src: Chapter 10 continues the series of feast sermons (see study note on 5:1–10:42). Here, the setting is the Feast of Dedication. The timing of this feast is important for understanding the story (see study note on 10:22).
text_es_aquifer: El Capítulo 10 continúa la serie de sermones festivos (ver nota de estudio sobre 5:1–10:42). Aquí, el escenario es Hanukkah (la Fiesta de la Dedicación), cuyo momento es crucial para entender la historia (ver nota de estudio sobre 10:22).

text_src: ⸢the sheep listen for his voice⸣: The Middle Eastern shepherd is well known for having intimate knowledge of the sheep. Sheep are led with flute tunes, songs, or verbal commands.
text_es_aquifer: "las ovejas reconocen su voz": El pastor del Medio Oriente es bien conocido por tener un conocimiento íntimo de las ovejas. Las ovejas son guiadas con melodías de flauta, canciones o comandos verbales.

text_src: A good shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and leads them. He does not force them from behind. When the sheep recognize his voice, they trust him and follow.
text_es_aquifer: Un buen pastor siempre guía a sus ovejas; nunca las empuja. Cuando reconocen su voz, confían en su liderazgo y lo siguen.

text_src: I am: See study note on 6:35. A good shepherd protects the sheep at the gate like a guard.
text_es_aquifer: "Yo Soy": Ver nota de estudio en 6:35. Un buen pastor es conocido por proteger a las ovejas en la puerta como un centinela.

text_src: ⸢he will be saved⸣ (or ⸢will find safety⸣): As the guard at the gate, Jesus protects his sheep from harm by keeping them safe inside the pen.
text_es_aquifer: "serán salvados" (o "encontrarán seguridad"): Como guardián, Jesús mantiene alejados a aquellos que podrían dañar a sus ovejas, manteniendo a sus ovejas dentro del corral donde están seguras.

text_src: The followers of Jesus must be wary of bad shepherds who desire to ⸢steal and kill and destroy⸣. When they told the story of the Feast of Dedication to the Jewish people, it reminded them of false religious leaders (see study note on 10:22). The failures of these leaders had led to the loss of God's temple in Jerusalem during the time of the Maccabean Revolt.
text_es_aquifer: Los seguidores de Jesús deben estar atentos a los malos pastores que desean robar, matar y destruir. Al contar la historia de Hanukkah al pueblo judío (ver nota de estudio en 10:22), se les recordó sobre los falsos líderes religiosos cuyas fallas habían llevado a la pérdida del Templo de Dios en Jerusalén.

text_src: Small villages often created communal flocks and employed a hired hand to tend the sheep. However, an employee lacked the commitment of a true shepherd. The wilderness of Judea had many predators. When a wolf or other predators attacked, the hired hand would run rather than defend the sheep. Jesus will never do this; he will always stand between his sheep and danger.
text_es_aquifer: Las pequeñas aldeas a menudo creaban rebaños comunales y empleaban a un jornalero para cuidar las ovejas. Sin embargo, un empleado carecía del compromiso de un verdadero pastor. El desierto de Judea tenía muchos depredadores. Cuando un lobo u otros depredadores atacaban, el jornalero huía en lugar de defender a las ovejas. Jesús nunca hará esto; él siempre se interpondrá entre sus ovejas y el peligro.

text_src:
⸢I am⸣: See study note on 6:35. The good shepherd guides his sheep, finds food and water, and locates paths in the wilderness (see Psalm 23). The good shepherd stands between his sheep and danger (John 10:11). 

The Old Testament describes God as Israel’s shepherd (Psalms 23; 80:1; Isaiah 40:10–11). The religious leaders of God’s people should care for their flock as God does (Ezekiel 34:23). However, the leaders of Israel in the time of Jesus were not good shepherds.
text_es_aquifer: "Yo Soy": Ver nota de estudio en 6:35. El buen pastor guía a sus ovejas, encuentra comida y agua, y localiza caminos en el desierto (ver Sal 23). El buen pastor se interpone entre sus ovejas y el peligro (Juan 10:11) y lucha para protegerlas. El Antiguo Testamento describe a Dios como el pastor de Israel (Sal 23, 80:1, Is 40:10–11). Los líderes del pueblo de Dios deben pastorear su rebaño como lo hace Dios (Ez 34:23). Sin embargo, los líderes de Israel en la época de Jesús eran malos pastores.

lemma_src: I give my life for the sheep
text_src: ⸢I give my life for the sheep⸣: Jesus was speaking about his coming death. He was referring to his crucifixion (his death on a cross; chapter 19).
text_es_aquifer: "Sacrifico mi vida por las ovejas": Jesús estaba aludiendo a su crucifixión (cap. 19).

text_src: The Father and the Son have an intimate relationship. Jesus shares a similar relationship with his sheep (his followers) through the Holy Spirit (14:23–31; 15:1–11).
text_es_aquifer: El Padre y el Hijo comparten una profunda intimidad, que Jesús comparte con sus ovejas a través del Espíritu Santo (14:23–31, 15:1–11).

text_src: ⸢other sheep⸣: Jesus spoke about sheep who were not part of the present sheepfold. This refers to people outside Judaism who would later believe in him (see 11:52). The followers of Jesus would not be divided by ethnic background. Jewish and Gentile believers from many cultures would become one flock. There would be one shepherd and one united people (17:20–23).
text_es_aquifer: "otras ovejas": Los creyentes fuera del judaísmo un día se unirían al redil de Jesús (ver 11:52). En la visión de Jesús para su pueblo, los creyentes judíos y gentiles de diversas culturas se convertirían en un solo rebaño con un solo pastor (17:20–23).

text_src: ⸢No one takes it from Me⸣: The death of the Son was voluntary. Jesus was not a helpless victim of events beyond his control. He chose to give his life freely in obedience and close relationship with the Father (see Acts 2:23–24). The resurrection of Jesus was not an afterthought or a rescue from failure. God cannot be confined by death or a tomb. Because Jesus and the Father are one, Jesus possessed the authority to rise from death.
text_es_aquifer: "Nadie puede quitarme la vida": La muerte del Hijo fue voluntaria. Jesús no fue una víctima indefensa de acontecimientos que escapaban a su control. Su decisión de morir fue dada libremente en obediencia y relación íntima con su Padre (ver Hechos 2:23–24). • La resurrección de Jesús no fue una ocurrencia tardía en la que Dios rescató a su Hijo de la tragedia. Dios no podía ser retenido por una tumba, y como Jesús y el Padre son uno, Jesús poseía la autoridad para resucitar de la muerte.

text_src: Jesus divided his audience yet again (see also 6:66–69; 7:43; 9:16). His words and actions led people to one of two responses: opposition or faith.⸢He is demon-possessed⸣: Compare 7:20; 8:48–49, 52.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús dividió a su audiencia una vez más (ver también 6:66–69, 7:43, 9:16), inspirando ya sea oposición o fe. • "Está poseído por un demonio": Cf. 7:20, 8:48–49, 52.

text_src:
⸢the Feast of Dedication⸣: This winter feast is also known as Hanukkah. It celebrates the time when the Jews rededicated the temple after Antiochus IV (175–163 BC) defiled it in. Two hundred years before Jesus was born, Greek soldiers captured the Jerusalem Temple, stole its treasures, and made it unusable for worship. 

In the winter of 165–164 BC, a Jewish army led by Judas Maccabeus reclaimed the temple and rededicated it to the Lord. The Feast of Hanukkah ("⸢dedication⸣") celebrates this event (see ⸢1 Maccabees⸣ 3–4; ⸢2 Maccabees⸣ 8:1–10:8). 

During the feast, priests examined their commitment to service, using Ezekiel 34 as their main text for reflection (also Jeremiah 23:1–4; 25:32–38; Zechariah 11). At this Hanukkah celebration, Jesus used the shepherd theme from Ezekiel 34 to show he was the good shepherd (John 10:11). He also showed how Israel’s current religious leaders were bad shepherds (10:10, 12–13).
text_es_aquifer: Hanukkah era un festival de invierno que conmemoraba la rededicación del Templo después de que había sido profanado por Antíoco IV (175–163 a.C.). Doscientos años antes de Cristo, soldados griegos capturaron y saquearon el Templo de Jerusalén, tomaron sus tesoros y artefactos, y lo hicieron inutilizable para el culto. En el invierno de 165–164 a.C., un ejército judío liderado por Judas Macabeo recuperó el Templo y lo rededicó al Señor. El Festival de Hanukkah (“dedicación”) marcó esta dedicación (ver 1 Macabeos 3–4, 2 Macabeos 8:1–10:8). Durante el festival, los sacerdotes examinaban su compromiso con el servicio, usando Ezequiel 34 como su texto principal para la reflexión (también Jeremías 23:1–4, 25:32–38, Zacarías 11). En esta celebración de Hanukkah, Jesús utilizó el tema del pastor de Ezequiel 34 para distinguirse entre él mismo como el buen pastor (Juan 10:11) y los líderes religiosos de Israel de su tiempo como malos pastores (10:10, 12–13).

text_src:
Large covered walkways with rows of columns stood around all four sides of the temple’s central courtyard. These structures are called colonnades.

Solomon’s Colonnade was on the east side. It provided shelter from wind and rain, especially during the winter months.
text_es_aquifer: Los cuatro lados del patio central del Templo estaban rodeados por pórticos cubiertos. La columnata de Salomón⸢,⸣ al este, proporcionaba refugio del clima invernal.

text_src: The people around Jesus might have been trying to understand, or they might have been hostile. In Luke 21:20 and Hebrews 11:30, the same word describes how armies surrounded Jerusalem and Jericho before their destruction. In Acts 14:20, it refers to Paul's disciples gathering around him after he was injured.
text_es_aquifer: Las personas que rodeaban a Jesús podrían haber estado buscando claridad, o podrían haber sido hostiles. En Lucas 21:20 y Hebreos 11:30, la misma palabra describe cómo Jerusalén y Jericó fueron rodeadas antes de ser destruidas; en Hechos 14:20 la referencia es a los discípulos de Pablo reuniéndose a su alrededor después de haber sido herido.

text_src: Jesus had already provided the Jewish people and their religious leaders with sufficient proof that he is the Son of God. The problem was not lack of information, but their unwillingness to believe him.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús ya había proporcionado al pueblo judío y a sus líderes religiosos pruebas suficientes de que él era el Hijo de Dios. El problema no era la falta de información, sino su falta de disposición para creerle.

text_src:
In his final public statement in this Gospel, Jesus gave a clear and complete declaration about who he is (10:30). He spoke openly about his unity with the Father.

This statement brought his public teaching to a high point and made his identity unmistakable.
text_es_aquifer: En la última presentación pública de pruebas sobre sí mismo en este Evangelio, Jesús da un testimonio exhaustivo de su identidad (10:30).

text_src: As the good shepherd, Jesus would die for his sheep and protect them from all predators and thieves (10:1, 8, 11; see Ezekiel 34:22–23). The Father's power, shown through Jesus, keeps his sheep safe. No one can steal from Jesus those who trust in him. This is because no one is stronger than Jesus. Their security depends on Christ, not their own efforts. The word translated as ⸢snatch⸣ suggests violence (as in John 6:15).
text_es_aquifer: Como el buen pastor, Jesús moriría por sus ovejas y las protegería de todos los depredadores y ladrones (10:1, 8, 11; cp. Ezequiel 34:22–23). • El poder del Padre⸢,⸣ que aparece en Cristo, mantiene a sus ovejas seguras. Los creyentes no pueden ser arrebatados de Jesús porque nadie es más poderoso que él. La seguridad de quienes creen no se sostiene por sus propios esfuerzos, sino por Cristo. • La palabra traducida como "arrebatar" implica violencia (como en Juan 6:15).

text_src:
The Father and the Son are distinct persons, yet they share one purpose and one divine nature (1:1, 14; 14:9; 20:28). They are not the same person. Yet they are united in will, authority, and being.

Because of this unity, Jesus has the power to protect God’s flock (10:28–29). His words are a strong statement about his divinity.
text_es_aquifer: El Padre y el Hijo son dos personas separadas con un propósito y naturaleza únicos (1:1, 14; 14:9, 20:28). Esta es la base del poder de Jesús para proteger el rebaño de Dios (10:28–29) y una impresionante expresión de su divinidad.

text_src: The people understood what Jesus meant and wanted to kill him (see 10:33). The problem was not that Jesus performed good works, but that he claimed to be God (see 6:42, 60; 7:29–30). Blasphemy (speaking in a way that dishonors God) was punishable by death under the law of Moses. The required punishment was stoning (see Leviticus 24:23; John 8:59).
text_es_aquifer: La gente entendió el significado de Jesús (ver 10:33) y quería matarlo. El problema no eran sus buenas obras⸢,⸣ sino su afirmación de divinidad (ver 6:42, 60; 7:29–30). Cometer blasfemia era castigado con apedreamiento (Lv 24:23; ver Jn 8:59).

text_src: ⸢‘I have said you are gods’⸣: If the word ⸢gods⸣ could describe people other than the Lord, then Jesus was not breaking the law by referring to himself in this way. But Jesus is not just any son of God. Jesus is ⸢the⸣ ⸢Son of God⸣ who ⸢the Father⸣ sent into the world.
text_es_aquifer: "¡Yo digo, ustedes son dioses!" Si la palabra dios pudiera aplicarse a personas distintas del Señor, entonces Jesús no estaba quebrantando la ley al referirse a sí mismo de esta manera. Sin embargo, Jesús no es solo cualquier hijo de Dios; es el Hijo de Dios que fue enviado . . . al mundo.

text_src: The miraculous works Jesus performed should help true believers know and understand that the full reality of God dwells in Jesus.
text_es_aquifer: Las obras milagrosas de Jesús deberían ayudar a los verdaderos creyentes a saber y entender que la plena realidad de Dios habita en Jesús.

text_src: His revelation to the Jewish leaders now complete, Jesus went to the region beyond the Jordan River where John the Baptist had once worked and where Jesus was baptized.
text_es_aquifer: Con su revelación a los líderes judíos ahora completa, Jesús se retiró a la región más allá del río Jordán donde Juan el Bautista había trabajado una vez y donde Jesús fue bautizado.

lemma_src: everything he said about this man was true
text_src: ⸢everything he said about this man was true⸣: See 1:19–51; 3:22–36. The fulfillment of John the Baptist’s predictions confirms both that he was a prophet and that what he said about Jesus was true.
text_es_aquifer: "todo lo que dijo sobre este hombre se ha hecho realidad": Ver 1:19–51, 3:22–36. El cumplimiento de las predicciones de Juan el Bautista confirma tanto que él era un profeta como que lo que dijo sobre Jesús era verdad.

text_src: This is a note of irony (an unexpected contrast). In Jerusalem, the holy city, Jesus found little faith among the religious leaders. But in the desert, away from the center of religious power, many people believed in him.
text_es_aquifer: Esta es una nota de ironía. Mientras Jesús encontró poca fe entre los líderes religiosos en la ciudad santa de Jerusalén, en el desierto encontró a muchos que … creían.

text_src: In the Hebrew language, ⸢Lazarus⸣ is a shortened form of ⸢Eleazar⸣, which means "God helps." In the first century, it was the fourth most common name for Jewish men (see also Luke 16:19–31). Bethany was a small village east of Jerusalem, just past the Mount of Olives (John 11:18). Jesus often stayed there when he visited Jerusalem. He likely traveled through Bethany on his way to Jerusalem. This was because most Jews from Galilee took a route going south to Jericho, then west to Jerusalem. Mary and Martha were sisters (see Luke 10:38–42). Martha was probably older. She was the host in Luke’s Gospel and represented the family. Mary later anointed Jesus with perfume (John 12:1–8).
text_es_aquifer: En hebreo, Lázaro es una forma abreviada de ⸢Eleazar⸣ (“Dios ayuda”). Entre los judíos del primer siglo, era el cuarto nombre más común para un hombre (ver también Lucas 16:19–31). • Betania era un pequeño pueblo al este de Jerusalén, justo sobre el Monte de los Olivos (Juan 11:18) y era donde Jesús a menudo se quedaba cuando estaba en la ciudad santa. Así, habría viajado a través de Betania en el camino a Jerusalén porque la mayoría de los judíos que venían de Galilea usaban una ruta que iba al sur hacia Jericó, y luego al oeste hacia Jerusalén. • María y Marta eran hermanas (Lucas 10:38–42). Marta probablemente era mayor; era la anfitriona en la historia de Lucas y aquí representaba a la familia. María más tarde ungió a Jesús con perfume (Juan 12:1–8).

text_src:
The resurrection of Lazarus points to the future death and resurrection of Jesus. The description of Lazarus’s tomb is similar to the description of the tomb Jesus was placed in after he died (11:38, 44; 20:1, 7). Both accounts mention a cave and burial cloths. These details connect the two events and help us see that Lazarus’s story is a sign.

Soon after Lazarus was raised, a woman anointed Jesus for burial (12:3). This act prepared him for his coming death.

Then the time for his glorification began (12:23).
text_es_aquifer: La resurrección de Lázaro presagia la propia muerte y resurrección de Jesús. Incluso la descripción de la tumba de aquel (11:38, 44) prefigura la tumba de Jesús (20:1, 7). Poco después de este evento, Jesús fue ungido para el entierro (12:3) y comenzó la hora de su glorificación (12:23).

text_src: The two sisters had a difficult choice to make. They knew Jesus was able to heal, but they also realized that his return to Judea would involve personal risk (11:8).
text_es_aquifer: Las dos hermanas tenían un dilema. Conocían el poder de Jesús como sanador, pero también se dieron cuenta de que su regreso a Judea implicaría un riesgo personal (11:8).

text_src: Jesus responded with words that were similar to his words about the man born blind (9:1–5). Jesus already knew Lazarus was dead (11:14). He was talking about Lazarus's resurrection, which would bring glory to God (11:43).
text_es_aquifer: La respuesta de Jesús hizo paralelo de sus palabras sobre el hombre nacido ciego (9:1–5). Jesús ya sabía que Lázaro estaba muerto (11:14); estaba hablando sobre la resurrección de Lázaro (11:43), lo cual traería gloria a Dios.

text_src: The trip to Bethany from where Jesus was staying would have taken only one day (see 10:40). However, Jesus followed his own timing and did not let others rush him (2:4; 7:5–9).
text_es_aquifer: El viaje desde donde Jesús se quedaba (ver 10:40) hasta Betania habría tomado solo un día, pero él siguió su propio sentido del tiempo (2:4, 7:5–9) y no se dejaría influenciar por otros.

text_src: The disciples were rightly worried about the risk (see 7:25; 8:37, 44, 59; 10:31, 39).
text_es_aquifer: Los discípulos estaban preocupados por el riesgo con razón (ver 7:25, 8:37, 44, 59; 10:31, 39).

text_src: ⸢Thomas⸣: See also 14:5; 20:24; 21:2; Mark 3:18. ⸢Let us also go, so that we may die⸣: Thomas knew that earlier visits to Judea had been risky (John 5:18; 10:31, 39). Traveling to Jerusalem now would likely mean death for Jesus (compare 11:49–50).
text_es_aquifer: "Tomás": Ver también 14:5, 20:24, 21:2, Marcos 3:18. • "Vamos también y muramos": Tomás sabía que las visitas anteriores a Judea habían sido peligrosas (Juan 5:18, 10:31, 39). Viajar a Jerusalén ahora probablemente significaría la muerte para Jesús (cf. 11:49–50).

text_src:
In Jewish custom at that time, people were usually buried on the same day they died. Families placed the body in a tomb quickly, often within hours.

John tells us that Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days. This detail is important. It shows that Lazarus was truly dead.

Because four days had passed, this miracle was not a simple resuscitation (bringing someone back who only seemed dead). Jesus did not restore a weak person who might recover. He raised a man who had been dead and buried for several days.
text_es_aquifer: Las personas eran enterradas el mismo día de su muerte. Juan notó que Lázaro había estado en su tumba durante cuatro días⸢,⸣ por lo que el milagro no podía interpretarse como una resucitación.

text_src: Life in New Testament times was lived publicly. Lazarus’s large extended family, as well as the villagers, had arrived for a seven-day mourning period. To console the sisters in their loss, there was great wailing and crying (see 11:33 and corresponding study note).
text_es_aquifer: La vida en los tiempos del Nuevo Testamento se vivía públicamente. La gran familia extendida de Lázaro, así como los aldeanos, habían llegado para un período de duelo de siete días. Para consolar a las hermanas en su pérdida, hubo grandes lamentos y llantos (ver 11:33 y la nota de estudio correspondiente).

text_src: ⸢Lord, if You had been here⸣: Mary later repeated Martha’s words (11:32), because both sisters knew that Jesus had a reputation as a healer. They concluded that Jesus would have healed Lazarus, but they did not imagine that Jesus would restore him from death.
text_es_aquifer: "Señor, si hubieras estado aquí": María repitió más tarde las palabras de Marta (11:32), porque ambas hermanas conocían la reputación de Jesús como sanador. Concluyeron que Jesús habría sanado a Lázaro, pero no imaginaron que Jesús lo resucitaría de entre los muertos.

text_src: ⸢whatever You ask of Him⸣: Martha believed Jesus could still help in some way. Despite this, she objected when Jesus wanted to open the tomb (11:39). She did not think Jesus would resurrect her brother from the dead.
text_es_aquifer: "lo que pidas": Marta pensó que Jesús aún podría intervenir de alguna manera. A pesar de esto, ella se opuso cuando Jesús quiso abrir la tumba (11:39); no pensaba que Jesús resucitaría a su hermano de entre los muertos.

text_src: ⸢rise again in the resurrection at the last day⸣: Martha misunderstood Jesus because she thought he meant the general resurrection of all dead people at the end of time (compare 11:11–13).
text_es_aquifer: "cuando todos los demás se levanten, en el último día": Marta lo malinterpretó (cp. 11:11–13), pensando que Jesús se refería a la resurrección general de los muertos al final de los tiempos.

lemma_src: I am the resurrection and the life
text_src: Jesus helped Martha believe in him not only as someone who heals, but as someone who defeats death. ⸢I am the resurrection and the life⸣: Victory over death comes from living in union with Jesus. Although the followers of Jesus will one day die, they will have eternal life after death. For more on the ⸢I am⸣ statements of Jesus, see the study note on 6:35.
text_es_aquifer: Jesús ayudó a Marta a creer en él no simplemente como un sanador, sino como alguien que vence la muerte. • "Yo soy la resurrección y la vida": la victoria sobre la muerte es un aspecto de vivir en asociación con Jesús. Aunque sus seguidores aún son mortales, disfrutarán de la vida eterna después de la muerte. En cuanto a las declaraciones "Yo soy" de Jesús, ver la nota de estudio sobre 6:35.

text_src:
⸢Do you believe this?⸣: Jesus was not simply asking Martha if he could bring Lazarus out of the grave. Martha already believed that Lazarus would rise again on the last day.

Instead, Jesus asked a deeper question. Did Martha believe that life itself is connected to him?“⸢Yes, Lord⸣”: Even though she did not fully understand, she acknowledged that Jesus was the Christ, God's chosen one. But she was still surprised by his power.
text_es_aquifer: "¿Crees esto?" Jesús no estaba preguntándole a Marta si creía que podía sacar a Lázaro de la tumba. Más bien, ¿creía ella que la vida misma estaba vinculada a Jesús? • “Sí, Señor”: Aunque las implicaciones completas estaban más allá de su comprensión, reconoció que Jesús era de hecho el Mesías. Sin embargo, se sorprendió del poder que él tenía.

text_src: Mary now joined the scene on the edge of the village, repeating her sister’s cry of misery. She fell at the feet of Jesus, not in worship but in desperate grief.
text_es_aquifer: María ahora se unió a la escena en el límite del pueblo, repitiendo el llanto lastimero de su hermana. Y cayó a los pies de Jesús, no en adoración sino en desesperado dolor.

text_src: Loud ⸢weeping⸣ and crying out were common public displays of grief in this culture, as was beating one's chest (Mark 5:38; Luke 18:13). The Greek word translated ⸢deeply moved in spirit⸣ describes strong human emotion, including outrage or anger. Jesus was not angry at Martha or Mary. Jesus was angry because the situation showed the people’s lack of belief, even though resurrection was real and near.
text_es_aquifer: El llanto y los lamentos fuertes eran típicos de las demostraciones públicas de dolor en esta cultura (Marcos 5:38), al igual que golpearse el pecho (Lucas 18:13). • La palabra griega traducida como "profunda ira" expresa indignación humana, furia y enojo. Jesús estaba furioso, no con Marta o María, sino con la futilidad de esta escena y la incredulidad de la gente ante la realidad de la resurrección.

text_src: Lazarus was buried in a tomb cut from the rocky hillside; such tombs were common. The tomb was closed and opened for further burials with a rolling stone that covered the entrance. A central door led to a cave room where burial benches were carved in stone along the inner wall. Horizontal burial chambers were cut along the top edge of the benches.
text_es_aquifer: Lázaro fue enterrado en una tumba excavada en la ladera rocosa; estas tumbas eran comunes. La tumba se cerraba y abría para más entierros con una piedra rodante que cubría la entrada. Una puerta central conducía la sala de la cueva donde había bancos funerarios tallados en piedra a lo largo de la pared interior. Y cámaras funerarias horizontales estaban cortadas a lo largo del borde superior de estos.

text_src: News of the miracle quickly spread to Jerusalem (12:9, 17). Again, people had different opinions about who Jesus was (6:66–69; 7:43; 9:16; 10:19; 11:37). Jesus was famous in Galilee for healing and raising the dead (see Matthew 9:24–26; 10:8; 11:5). Now he had brought this power to Judea.
